speakeroldname: Hon. Gilles Loiselle (President of the TVeasury Board and Minister of State (Finance)) moved
speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext: that Bill C-3, an act respecting the acquisition, administration and disposition of real property by the Government of Canada be now read a second time and referred to Legislative Committee F.

speakeroldname: Mr. Bill Kempling (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the TVeasury Board and Minister of State (Finance)):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Finance); Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, recently the President of the Treasury Board introduced a bill in this House, Bill C-3,
October 7, 1991

an act respecting the acquisition, administration and disposition of federal real property.
I am pleased to be here today to lead off debate on this bill, as we seek to consolidate the policy changes and the new procedures associated with the government's reform of its real property management system.
Five years ago the government was faced with a real property system, some would say lack of a system, under which it was very difficult to know which minister of the Crown had responsibility for which property and for what purpose. Since then, substantial progress has been made. The goal of reform is to improve the effectiveness of the federal land management. When I say land, I refer not only to undeveloped land, but also to land complete with buildings.
To improve management of the federal real property, the cabinet first approved a new regime based on decentralization of authority to the departments that use the property for delivery of services to Canadians. We have cut the red tape to save money, to reduce overhead, and to improve the service to the public. In other words, we moved to modernize the way real property is managed in the government.
We made Treasury Board ministers a focal point for policy and general management decisions. This establishes the decentralization of management work by providing managers in the field with clear lines of accountability.
We have clarified the role of Public Works Canada as manager of federal office buildings and as a source of specialized services to other departments.
We shifted responsibility for the administration of most special buildings, or facilities such as laboratories, to the individual departments actually using those facilities.
The result is a very highly decentralized system with authority and accountability vested in program departments, rather than central agencies, and administered by local property managers, not Ottawa.
The special group known as the Bureau of Real Property Management was set up within the Treasury Board secretariat to manage and co-ordinate the process of decentralization, as well as providing advice to the
Government Orders
Treasury Board ministers on their new role in looking after real property.
With these important reforms in place, we turned our attention to the method used for federal real property conveyancing. Bill C-3 is one of the last steps needed to complete the simplification and modernization of the way federal lands and buildings are managed.
The federal real property management act will bring together, in one statute, the general authorities necessary to buy, sell or lease the lands and buildings used by government departments to deliver the programs to the Canadian public. It would enable the government to use the same means to buy or sell property that are used by the private sector, but with appropriate controls in place. This would make it faster and easier for the private sector to deal with the government. It would increase efficiency in property transactions, reduce delays, and eliminate differences in approach that now exist between the government and the private sector. In Alberta, we will be able to do things the Albertan way and in Ontario, the way they do things in Ontario, and so on.
The bill would give the government the flexibility it needs to be an efficient manager of real property. It would improve service to the public in a significant way by allowing the government to use modem methods in dealing with Canadians when it buys, sells, leases or transfers lands or buildings.
I am pleased to submit these proposals to the House today. However useful they may be, these proposals are strictly limited in scope. Let me explain. First, they would not affect the management of lands governed by special legislation such as the Indian Act, the National Parks Act or the Territorial Lands Act. In each case, the specialized legislation would override the federal real property act. Nor would these proposals affect the management of lands held by Crown corporations. These corporations would continue to manage properties in support of their commercial and public policy objectives, under their own legislation, or under the Financial Administration Act.
The federal real property act would, however, apply to the property transactions of about 20 departments of the federal Public Service that hold land for delivery of programs to Canadians. The diversity of these holdings would surprise you, Mr. Speaker, covering everything

October 7, 1991
Government Orders
from cultural centres to defence bases, employment centres, nursing stations, research labs, farms, airports, prisons, police detachments, embassies, consulates and about 25,000 residences in Canada and around the world. About 85 per cent of these facilities are outside of Ottawa.
The vast majority of this property is devoted to providing direct service to the public. It represents the full range of facilities needed to deliver the federal government services to the Canadian public. The federal government is the largest real property holder in Canada. We control a large, diverse and complex portfolio of real estate. Excluding the territories, we manage some 28 million square metres of building space and about 23 million hectares of land. If all this land was put in one place, it would cover about the same area as Great Britain. The sheer number, and diversity, of federal land holdings makes for thousands of property transactions a year. That is why it was absolutely necessary that decision making and managerial accountability be decentralized. That is why legislation to support this improved management structure must keep pace.
The new regime for real property management is in keeping with our overriding goal of improving services to the public. It gives the managers more direct responsibility and holds them accountable for the results.
Under the present law many, if not most, real property decisions concern acquisitions, and purchases must come from Ottawa. The decision making process is highly centralized. The proposed legislation would allow the government to delegate these decisions outside Ottawa where it makes good business sense to do so.
Currently, three separate and often conflicting statutes govern the way real property transactions are handled. These statutes are the Public Lands Grants Act, the Public Works Act (Part II) and the Surplus Crown Assets Act. These acts are complex and out of date.
The Public Lands Grants Act and Part II of the Public Works Act as they apply to real estate transactions are essentially unchanged from the 1890s. That is the 1890s, Mr. Speaker.
We have been operating with a real policy regime designed for the horse and buggy era dealing with assets that are virtually priceless, and that belong to all taxpayers of Canada. It is clearly time that this obsolete legislation be modernized.
The third piece of legislation, the Surplus Crown Assets Act, was designed to deal primarily with surplus office furniture and equipment, not with lands. It is inadequate to deal with real property.
These statutes do not allow the use of modem real property methods or practices similar to those followed in the private sector. They use different terms to describe the same things and they use different mechanisms to carry out the same kind of transactions. Under these old laws, selling even a small piece of property can take from six to nine months after a decision has been made.
Take, for example, the sale of a modest house that used to serve as the residence of an RCMP officer in a remote British Columbia detachment. Today the house has outlived its usefulness and the RCMP has decided that it should be sold. Under the present rules, it would probably take the agreement of two cabinet committees and processing by as many as five government departments, over a period of six to nine months, to complete the sale. Most of the work would be done in Ottawa, far from the local market, with the attendant risk of errors.
You could imagine the headache that this kind of transaction causes Canadians across the country trying to buy property from the federal government.
With the flexibility of the proposed new act the same transaction would take six to eight weeks, that is, 60 or 80 per cent faster, and involve a British Columbia-based RCMP official and a local Department of Justice lawyer.
I trust you will agree, Mr. Speaker, that this is much better than six to nine months, and a big improvement in service to the public.
Similarly, under the law, it is no easy matter to surrender a lease, even in situations in which a terminating lease is beneficial to the tenant, and to the government. Managers in the field do not have the authority necessary to make the decision.
October 7, 1991

Let us say that a concessionaire in Halifax International Airport wishes to relocate to larger premises in the same building. The government agrees that the new space rents for more money and a new tenant is already waiting for the old premises. At present, because this move involves the surrender of an existing lease, the decision can only be made with the approval of the Governor in Council, on the recommendation of the Treasury Board, on a submission by the Minister of Transport. Obviously this process is time consuming and is neither efficient nor service-oriented.
For the most part, the legislation we are proposing today clarifies, codifies and simplifies existing practices in legislation to ensure good management of real property transactions such as the procedures used to make transfers between ministers and between governments.
The proposed legislation clarifies the role of individual government departments with land holdings. The bill emphasizes that federal real property is a long-term asset of the people of Canada. Departments are the temporary stewards of the land they hold to deliver their programs.
The bill also clarifies the role of the Department of Justice in ensuring that the interests of the Government of Canada, and thus the people of Canada, are served in property transactions.
In conclusion, the provision of this bill would clarify and simplify the current arrangements for buying, selling, leasing, licensing and transferring federal real property. These measures are straightforward, as I have said. They are designed to eliminate inconsistencies between laws that treat similar transactions in different ways, and use modem methods in federal land transactions.
The passage of the proposed federal real property act would improve service to the public by reducing delays and frustration on the part of the public that deals with the government on property transactions. It would reduce the cost and increase the efficiency of how the government manages our properties.
For these reasons, I believe the passage of the proposed legislation will enable us to better manage the real property assets that we hold for all Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, Bill C-3 clearly reflects the government's desire to
Government Orders
simplify procedures in an area of administration that can be very complex, as the government member pointed out. All federal government land put together would cover roughly the same area as England. That is a lot of territory to manage, and in recent years, procedures had become very unwieldy.
When I was in the National Assembly, for instance, we had the same system we have here, and when there were "letters patent", it could take six or eight months to get them, if we were lucky. My point is that transactions of this kind do not reflect current procedures or transactions in the private sector, which is often a source of frustration.
The bill contains a number of elements that are most welcome, of course, but this is something that evolved gradually. There is a story behind those elements, and I would like to explain the reason for a bill of this scope. There may also be a few omissions that perhaps our government colleagues would be able to clarify.
Mr. Speaker, in 1985, the study team on real property management, established by the Ministerial Task Force on Program Review-there were an enormous number of programs, and this was under Mr. Nielsen, the minister at the time-this study team published a report that mentioned a number of shortcomings in management procedures for federal real property.
There were several recommendations for simplifying and updating the procedures then in effect, and these recommendations were subsequently adopted by Cabinet. Following Cabinet's decision, that same year Treasury Board set up the Bureau of Real Property Management responsible for co-ordinating management of the federal government's real property. With the co-operation of the Department of Justice and all responsible departments, the Bureau proceeded with a review of the instruments used to grant federal property.
The Bureau reported its findings, and I will mention some of these later on. The bill itself is fairly technical, and I would rather not get into the technical aspects. The three main bodies of legislation that governed federal real property conveyancing and which are currently in effect-the Public Lands Grants Act, the Public Works Act and the Surplus Crown Assets Act-no longer reflected current real property management methods and techniques. The first two have not changed much since they came into effect, that would be in the 1890s,

October 7, 1991
Government Orders
while the last one is better suited for disposing of personal property than real property.
These acts contain inconsistencies as regards the methods and procedures. They are redundant and thus are confusing for the people handling the transfers.
Finally, Bill C-3 was designed to correct the many deficiencies in the present system. This legislation intended to update and streamline the methods used in the administration and disposition of federal real property will give a clearer definition of management responsibilities regarding public lands. It will also be useful to codify and revise legal provisions concerning many similar real estate transactions, if not all.
Here is the question I want to ask my colleague opposite. From what I understood, this legislation will apply to all public lands. One of the weaknesses of the bill was that it was not clear that all Crown lands would be covered. So, Bill C-3 will repeal the entire Territorial Lands Act and amend the Public Works Act and the Surplus Crown Assets Act so as to exclude from the application of these acts real estate transactions covered by this legislation.
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member mentioned earlier some form of accountability on the part of management. That is what I want to hear about. Will the accountability of managers that is in this bill really be there in fact? In the past, many people had dealings with the federal government and when there was confusion-I admit that the laws governing Crown buildings and land are very confusing. It would be a good idea in the bill, and it is not clear, that is one of its weaknesses-Will accountability really be there in fact? It would be a good idea to clear up the confusion that has existed on many occasions.
I would also point out that with a single piece of legislation to manage all Crown lands and even buildings, no doubt this statutory authority will make it unnecessary to search through all the current legislation to see who has the last word. Indeed, with this bill, the statutory authority will be the departments' responsibility and managers will be responsible for ensuring that in every department, these transactions comply with all the requirements the government put in the bill. No doubt the time transactions take will be greatly reduced, as it
should be, because transactions these days must be done quickly-we are no longer in the 19th century, when they could take years. Modem methods today require the government to keep up to date in it real estate transactions.
But one of the weaknesses we were able to note is that the bill does not specify how the procedure will work. For example, there is no specification now of how an individual would go about acquiring Crown land or how a particular department that has extra property in a given place would market it. I would like to know if he intends in committee to elaborate on the procedure to be implemented and what the chances for an individual dissatisfied with the procedure, to lodge an appeal?
I would also like to know something else. Pursuant to section 16, paragraph one, the Governor on Council may appoint an ad hoc review committee to make a decision. We would want assurances that, in case of improprieties, this committee established under the authority of the Governor in Council could be called before this House.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I would like the government to tell us whether all Crown lands-indeed those the hon. member mentioned-will be covered by this bill, including all government leases on buildings? The hon. member talked about 28 million square meters of building space. The federal government is obviously both the biggest tenant and the biggest land owner. Those are the points we would like the government to clarify before this bill can pass third reading.

Mr. Speaker, it gives me pleasure to rise and speak to Bill C-3, the bill dealing with the real property of the federal government. It has taken great pains to indicate to us that this is a veiy technical bill that we should pass very quickly through the House. Right away that give us some concern, but for the most part we approve of the vast majority of this bill and we do not want to be obstructionist. I will touch on what we think are the key elements of the bill and some of the concerns we have, although few in number we believe major in content, and we hope that the government will see its way clear to approve a couple of amendments that we believe are necessary in this bill.

The size of the bill, as a couple of my colleagues have suggested, is immense. We are talking about office buildings, houses, parks, police detachments, consulates, dry docks, employment offices. We have no doubt the federal government is the largest land and building owner in this country. Am I to believe it is $60 billion and the expenditure per year in this area is $6 billion. We may be speaking of a bill of a highly technical nature, but indeed it is a bill that could impact on everybody in this country.
It has been told to us that some of the language is archaic and the act is arcane and it is a hundred and some years out-dated. One could ask the question that if it was that bad, why did we not get to it beforehand.
It reminds me as bit of the UI bill and that gives me some concern. It is very technical and complex. It has lots of regulations. It is irrelevant and impractical at times. But when you get down to it, the interpretations of the regulations can be indeed very important to ordinary Canadians.
Inconsequential? Certainly not. We have received a tremendous amount of assurances, including from the creator of the bill. When I spoke to the creator of the bill and asked him whether any of our amendments would be acceptable, he seemed quite concerned or upset that I would suggest amending his creation.
I can understand that. Things that I put together I do not wish people to tamper with either, especially since, like a sculptor, he spent two years putting this bill together. Again, we will be proposing some amendments to the bill.
As far as the technicalities of the bill are concerned, they do expedite the system and that is good. Anything that can go from eight months to eight weeks will benefit all of those people, especially those involved in real estate transactions.
I think it is important that we try to put in some case studies. In my own community, a disagreement between Transport Canada and Parks Canada actually delayed a project for over a year in the community. As a result of that delay in the project, they are suggesting there are no more funds for the project, which may or may not be true.
Government Orders
It points out that the civil servants themselves, interdepartmentally, have difficulty getting a transaction through the process. Any expediting of the process indeed will be a bonus.
They point out to us that in the internal process, there will be a great deal of accountability. What the process does not uncover, the Auditor General will uncover. What the Auditor General does not uncover, a minister will uncover.
That is the accountability process within the department. Our concern will be at the end of the transactions. Will there be any final accountability? What we are suggesting among other things: one, a land and building inventory which, much to my surprise and I am sure to millions of Canadians, we have not had in place. As I speak, we do not have an inventory of properties in place.
They again assure us that we are in the process of doing that and it will be ready in 1992. Again, you are begged to ask the question: Why not previously? If we have $60 billion of assets, surely we would want them listed. There is an inventory that we believe is coming into place, and that is good.
We are saying that at the end, there should be an accountability clause in place-call it what you will, a depository-for all of the transactions that are completed on a monthly basis or on a bi-monthly basis or whatever, I will leave that up to the government. There should be a depository so that a citizen who is concerned and a citizen who deals with any aspect of Canadian life, be he integrally involved in real estate or not, has access to the depository to find out what the transaction was about and who are the principals.
I understand there would have to be some confidentiality involved in this depository. The government has suggested to me that I can go through the Access to Information Act. May I say that that is a very onerous exercise even for someone who might understand that system.
If the government is truly concerned with accountability for what it does, it will put together and initiate a depository that is extremely available. If the system is squeaky clean as the government is suggesting it will be because of all of the checks and balances of the system, that is great.

October 7, 1991
Government Orders
We must not only be absolutely squeaky clean, but we must appear to be completely devoid of any possibility of a scandal, a land scandal or whatever. It is not unknown or foreign to some people, mainly past, who have become involved in some of the land dealings.
There has been some innuendo and even court cases as to whether or not all of the government officials had acted in a proper fashion.
This depository would provide that last line of defence, that last safeguard that would prevent any possibility or potential, we believe, for abuse of the process. My friend from Victoria asked had there been an extensive consultation process. I am not aware of one, so I will not suggest that there was not one, but there was no indication from all of the briefing that I had that a consultation process was in place or pursued. But I would suggest that probably those involved would endorse this. I think, for the most part, the intent and most of the content of the bill is positive in nature. We would prefer not to sully the bill or the creator of the bill with any amendments, but there is no indication of any sound rationale yet as to why they would not accept the amendments; in fact, there is some dialogue back and forth suggesting that, yes, we see your point. They are talking about discretion, and there is little discretion within the system, but when it comes down to the final ministerial discretion, that minister may indeed have a tremendous amount of discretion. There is some suggestion that the government may be able to tailor-make land dealings to the benefit of somebody-to a community, for instance. If you had access to property in a community, and the federal government would like to give this piece of property to a city for a minimal amount, like $1,1 think that is good. It could be a policy that could be beneficial to everybody and would give a boost to a community that might need a boost-disregarding the market value.
Once again, if we offered this discretion just carte blanche to a minister or to a group of people, this indeed could lead to the concerns we have already mentioned, that people would suggest that things were not exactly as they were and they were politically motivated to dispense of property and/or building. So, even a very positive aspect of the discretionary aspect of the bill could become negative.
It is unfortunate that bills of this nature have to be so complex and technical, and it certainly was an education for me to get into some of the real estate jargon and legalese. I do not fully comprehend all of those aspects but I do understand full well the content. The perception that I have after having spent many hours with this bill is that the only criticism remaining is the accountability at the end of it, which remains vague at best and probably not in place at all.
We have tried to be as positive as possible in describing what is in the bill and our concerns. I do have in my hand endless numbers of clippings dealing with the negative aspects of this bill. It has caused the government in the past-and not only this government but many governments, and many individuals-a great deal of grief. So, the potential is there for scandal. An ounce of prevention, indeed, is worth a pound of cure.
We are suggesting that the depository is a must, before this bill goes forward with the endorsation of the New Democratic Party.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for my friend from Sault Ste. Marie. The bill in subclause 16(2) outlines a set of regulations that the Governor in Council may make. This is a very comprehensive set of regulations which, as I understand it under the scheme of the legislation, is going to govern how real estate transactions of the federal government are to take place. Yet the previous subclause seems to give the Governor in Council the opportunity to simply opt out of any regulations made under the clause.
My friend referred to that in his comments, but I wonder if he would elaborate on the extent of the discretionary authority and particularly the differences between the provisions in this bill and the provisions of the Financial Administration Act which would seem to be more restrictive and, therefore, give this Parliament, if more restrictive, the assurance that the regulations in fact will be the things that govern. In particular, it is because regulations have a public process that they have to go through and if cabinet can simply walk past the regulations, it would seem to me that it might offer some undue scope for an abuse of the process contrary to the intention of Parliament.
October 7, 1991

Mr. Speaker, I thank my colleague for the technical question on this technical bill. I suppose it is important because that is probably an aspect of the bill that I did not perhaps spend enough time on, but that is, of course, another concern we have, probably the two major concerns.
If the government in fact is suggesting that all of these new regulations are necessary to address all the potential transactions of the federal government in real property dealings, it begs the question: Why is the opting out clause notwithstanding any regulations necessary?
I am told that under the previous act this opting out clause is there, but it has never been used. Again the question is: If it has never been used for one hundred and some years and it should not have to be used now and forever after, why is the opting out clause there? It touches on the discretionary aspect of the bill that I did highlight, that there is no discretion internally in the process that is excellent, but the government may opt out just by simply saying we opt out of all of the regulations that we have put in place. That is the way I understand that.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to make a few comments on this bill. First, I would congratulate my friend from Sault Ste. Marie, who has sat next to me throughout this Parliament, on his very clear and competent speech on this bill setting out our position on it.
I would like to, however, add a few comments of my own partly based on my experience from Victoria where we have substantial federal properties, some of them vacant and some of them used, and a series of problems have emerged in the experience that I have had over the last couple of years that this bill, I hope, in part addresses. I would like to see some assurances from the government that it will address others that do not seem now to be covered by the bill.
In the question I put to my friend from Sault Ste. Marie just before I rose to speak on the bill, he dealt with the issue of clause 16 and the opportunity the government has to opt out. He made the very persuasive point that this clause, giving the government the right to opt out, is justified by the government on the basis that it never used it.
It seems to me that we have here an example of almost a conflict of interest that sometimes emerges between the government as government and the majority in the
Government Orders
House of Commons, the government acting as the leader of the majority in the House of Commons.
It seems to me that we as parliamentarians, all of us on all sides of the House, because this is not a partisan bill, should be insisting that safeguards of the public interest be written into legislation. Too often the government gets persuaded by its public servants to approve an internal system which is easier to regulate internally and overlooks the need to protect the public interest by a process of public accountability.
Clause 16(1) for example could do with a simple amendment that at any time the Governor in Council intended to exercise its powers under clause 16(1), it must be required in advance to report to a parliamentary committee or some other form of process of that kind so that the spotlight of public attention would be on the transaction, and the government would be obliged to account in the court of public opinion and in the court of this Parliament for its intention to try to explain why it was going around the normal regulations and procedures.
I would endorse as well in that context the recommendation of the member for Sault Ste. Marie for a complete public inventory of federally owned lands. There are, as has already been noted in this debate, 60,000 buildings in this country owned by the federal government, many of them very substantial buildings, 23 million hectares. The annual expenditures on buildings is over $6 billion.
This is a massive public responsibility which the government has in the administration of its lands and buildings. It is all behind closed doors except for the various cumbersome methods of trying to get the details out. The accountability of the government for its management of public lands is a difficult thing for the public to achieve under the present system. This bill does nothing to address that question.
If there is to be an inventory of the government's lands and buildings by December 31 of this year, as the government has assured us, why should that not be part of the legislation? Why should it not be a simple requirement that the government maintain an inventory of all of its land and buildings and further that it maintain a public inventory and registrar of all the transactions? Those transactions are recorded in public land offices across the country. It would be no trick at all

Government Orders
for the government to simply duplicate that process in a federal depository of land transactions so that any land transaction that occurred could quickly come to the attention of any member of the public who sought it as a companion to a public inventory of federal government lands.
The practical result of this has come to us in the Victoria area. The Department of National Defence is a major land owner in the Victoria area. Huge lands, much of which, as far as I can surmise, is completely superfluous to the actual usage by the Department of National Defence.
I have been told that there is an inventory being made of this. Even within the government there are pressures from one department to try to take advantage of those lands for public purposes, for example, social housing. I notice the member for Don Mills is in the House. He was the the Minister of Housing and I know his interest had been to improve the availability of federal lands for housing. I know as well that that is a continuing interest of the government in seeking to have more lands available.
The Department of National Defence, with all its surplus lands simply says, apparently: "We may need this some day in the long run and you can't have it". All of that process operates internally to the government.
The time has come to get that out of the back rooms and into the public so that the public can participate in that discussion and departments such as the Department of National Defence are far more clearly held accountable for their stewardship of the lands they have.
In the chosen area of greater Victoria, there is an area called Rocky Point, a huge area of land, to which is adjacent a national marine park, a small park. It would be an extremely good and valuable use of those lands to turn them into a national park. A very small fraction of those lands are now used to store ammunition for the navy.
I am quite confident that there has been no rigorous look at whether those lands are surplus, no imaginative look. The Department of National Defence has hoarded those lands. It seems to me that if this bill is to afford
Canadians the assurances that the government says it does, this should be brought out into the public and an opportunity given to look at the extent of surplus lands to government uses and to have a more public process for reviewing surplus lands, having government departments accountable for their use of lands so we can possibly begin to achieve some of the other purposes for which public land and buildings are needed.
A final aspect I would like to address is another public interest in government lands, and that is heritage. There is, again, a good internal system in the government for determining which federal government properties have heritage value. The Federal Heritage Review Board does that job and from everything I can see, does it very well.
The result is that if any other department seeks to use designated federal heritage buddings, it must in effect have that question referred to the review board, and the board wdl pass judgment on that. That is a good internal process.
Again, it is a process which should be brought out into the open. There should be a statutory provision establishing the heritage review process. There should be a statutory provision that requires reference to the heritage review board whenever an officially designated budding is to be treated in some form or another by a federal department.
Again we have an example of that in Victoria, where there is a long standing property, Gonzales Hdl, which was used as the first weather station on the west coast and an observation station during World Wars I and II. That building is now largely surplus as a weather station for the meteorological service but it has great heritage value and has been designated heritage.
Another arm of the government has said the land around that budding is surplus and should be sold off for expensive luxury housing. That decision has all been internal. If the wishes of the people of Victoria were taken into account, the whole of that property would be preserved in the public domain.
There are negotiations going on to try to achieve that objective. It is important that, in support of the heritage aspects of the federal government's responsibdity, this be given some statutory recognition and this would be a very valuable bdl to do this.
October 7, 1991

I propose to be introducing shortly a Private Member's bill to lead to the establishment of a national heritage policy in this country and I will be including those provisions. It would be far more effective if the government took the leadership on this and included these kinds of provisions in this bill.
Heritage of our building in Canada could be achieved in a whole range of ways, including the government establishing a policy that federal heritage buildings which are excess be used by federal departments far more efficiently than they have been so that our heritage can be preserved and maintained.
Let me conclude with a final point with respect to the way in which the federal government approaches its neighbours in planning the use of federal government properties.
Given the nature of this country and the age of buildings, we are now seeing more and more redevelopment across the country. In our area we have Ogden Point, a large parcel of land, a very critical parcel of land on the entrance to Victoria harbour.
In the early days of the development of Victoria, these federal lands were predominantly used for shipping, for the receiving of goods and essentially for industrial use connected with the passage of goods and services through the port of Victoria.
Much of that usage is now becoming obsolete with the change of transportation systems and the changes in the economy. The Government of Canada now has a large piece of very critical land for the development in Victoria that is surplus. What we see, however, is that in the process of redevelopment, the federal government internally proceeding to reach conclusions about the best use of that land with minimal consultation with the local communities and the local municipalities.
That has been the past record. There are signs of improvement. In this case, Transport Canada is the department responsible for the lands and the office in Vancouver has been very forthcoming in beginning a consultative process with the municipality in Victoria, and beginning slowly and tentatively a process of consultation with the community. It is far too tentative, however, far too much dependent upon the good will of particular public servants in particular regions.
Government Orders
I think it is incumbent upon the government, as a manager of real property, to provide a far better statutory base for what is the general policy of the government, that it will not develop its own lands without consent from the local municipality. That is a general policy, but it is a policy which is also honoured at least as much in the breaches of the observance whenever there is a controversy.
In this Ogden Point land I was speaking about, the federal government agreed to the establishment of a heliport which was wanted by some people in the community, but was definitely not desired by others in the community, including the unanimous vote of the council of the city of Victoria. Despite the unanimous vote of the council of the city of Victoria, despite the feeling of the neighbours, the government went ahead with this use. That is simply wrong. It is not a process which should be followed, and it is a process which should be corrected in this bill.
We on this side have a number of concerns about the bill. We appreciate the great importance of improving the system of land transactions. We congratulate the authors of this bill for bringing it forward on that ground. It is an important bill. Anyone who has ever had to have any real estate dealings with the federal government knows that, and we wish to facilitate its adoption. We also want to hear from the government a response to our concerns on the issues that have been raised by the member for Sault Ste. Marie and myself. They are important concerns, ones that we think are shared by many others across this country who have had dealings in this area.
We would like to hear from the government that it is willing to entertain amendments to just tighten up the bill in this respect.

Mr. Speaker, I must admit I perhaps got caught up in the technicalities of the bill. I think the member for Victoria has made a very very good point for all members of Parliament and probably for all Canadians. He obviously has a good handle on what is going on in his own constituency.
I must admit I perhaps do not have that kind of handle, but it points out the impact that the bill could have. We should pay attention to it.

Government Orders
As he was speaking I was trying to say: Do I have any case points to relate? I remember the post office. There was a controversy over the post office as to who was going to renovate the post office. I believe it belonged to Public Works.
As soon as Public Works found out it was going to have to spend money, it said: "It does not belong to us. It belongs to Canada Post." I called Canada Post and it said: "It belongs to Public Works."
If the inventory is in place, it is still having problems. The member has pointed out that there are ramifications of this bill. Certainly, the process of which he spoke has unlimited potential. For instance, we should take a serious look in each constituency in this country with the municipality, the province and the federal government. We should look at our excess lands and get away from: "This is my turf and don't you dare come on to it" and look at it for the benefit of all Canadians.
There is unlimited financial potential. It still staggers my imagination that we could have $60 billion worth of real property in this country.
It is not a question but I would ask the member if he wants to react to what I said.

Mr. Speaker, I will certainly react to his modesty in suggesting that he may not be as aware of the problems of his own constituency.
My experience with the member for Sault Ste. Marie since he has come here is that he is one of the most indefatigable constituency members in the country. "Indefatigable" may not be a word in common usage in every part of Sault Ste. Marie, but it means extremely hard working and very knowledgeable about the problems in his constituency.
Beyond that, I think he simply reinforced the point that I have made. I will leave it at that, and I look forward to hearing from the government in response to some of the points that we have suggested.

Mr. Speaker, on the same point, I have to agree that nobody seems to have the pulse or grasp of these property holdings of the federal government.
I do believe that in committee one could favourably look at the public inventory over federal lands. I think that is a good proposal.
I am wondering since the last comment made by my friend from Victoria. Based on the definition in the bill, I think it is clause 2, the bill would only apply to properties belonging to the federal Crown or of which the federal Crown had power to dispose depending upon how one defines federal real property.
That remains for us to decide in committee. If the Crown corporations, for example, have ownership rights over their holdings, I do not think this bill would apply to these holdings and these properties would not be covered by this bill.
I wonder if the member could confirm this for me. Crown corporations have large holdings of properties in Canada. I am thinking of the national capital region. The National Capital Commission has large holdings.
CMHC in my riding has large holdings which it is intending to dispose of. Does this bill touch Crown corporations in the member's view?

Mr. Speaker, it does not. I and my colleague from Sault Ste. Marie with whom I have consulted agree it ought not to confuse the issue. There is a very distinct set of problems related to lands held by Crown corporations and the government in that capacity.
That is not to say there is not a need for taking a look at how Crown corporations in this country administer their lands and the governments over all responsibility for the administration of all the lands. I would not be surprised at all to find that there are surplus lands that might be used better, and that the government should be following that through.
I know Treasury Board has some functions in that area and has some people working at it. It probably could be done a lot better. I also agree with an earlier comment my hon. friend from Sault Ste. Marie made about the problems that sometimes occur in a relationship between the two.
In Victoria we have a post office building that is being changed around and Public Works has been very responsive in that case to the needs of the people of Victoria in trying to improve that building, but it is still like pulling teeth and it should be a public process with Crown corporations as well as with the federal government.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)
speechtext:
that Bill C-18, an Act to amend the Income Tax Act, the Canada Pension Plan, the Cultural Property Export and Import Act, the Income Tctx Conventions Interpretation Act, the Tax Court of Canada Act, the Unemployment Insurance Act, the Canada-Newfoundland Atlantic Accord Implementation Act, the Canada- Nova Scotia Offshore Petroleum Resources Accord Implementation Act and certain related Acts, be now read the second time and referred to Legislative Committee E.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I have the pleasure of presenting, for the consideration of this House on second reading, Bill C-18, An Act to Amend the Income T&x and related Acts.

This bill is, as I am sure hon. members will appreciate, significant in both its physical size and its scope. It includes income tax measures from the 1990 and 1991 budgets, several items announced through press releases in 1990 and 1991, and a large number of technical amendments.
Since the measures were first announced, extensive consultations have taken place between the Department of Finance and taxpayers and their advisers on the more
Government Orders
technical aspects of this bill. These consultations have been of great help in identifying ways in which the details of the income tax system could be improved. Those improvements, together with the other amendments included in Bill C-18, will help to maintain and enhance the tax system's equity and efficiency. This goal, in turn, forms an important part of the government's commitment to a healthy Canadian economy.
I would now like to describe some of the major features of this bill, beginning with those income tax measures which form part of the budget brought down by the Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and International Trade, the former Minister of Finance, on February 20, 1990. These measures relate to the taxation of non-residents and life insurers, donations of Canadian cultural property, pension plans and registered education savings plans.
A basic element of the government's tax policy is the fair taxation of all income earned in Canada. The 1990 budget included initiatives to ensure that non-residents who deal in Canadian real estate or who create mutual funds to invest in Canadian real estate are taxed appropriately. The budget also proposed that the tax on financial institutions, introduced as part of tax reform, will be extended to life insurance companies. All of these measures have been incorporated in Bill C-18.
A second 1990 budget item relates to gifts of cultural property. In order to encourage the developments and dissemination of Canadian culture, the Income Tax Act provides special tax treatment for persons who donate cultural property to certain Canadian institutions or public authorities.
Bill C-18 will enhance the role of the Canadian Cultural Property Export Review Board in assessing the value of such property, and will thus streamline the rules governing cultural donations.
A third 1990 budget measure concerns pension funds. For many Canadians, retirement planning centres on a pension fund which invests their own, and their employers' contributions, to provide future income. Before 1990, such funds were subject to a special tax if more than 10 per cent of their assets consisted of foreign

October 7, 1991
Government Orders
property. Recognizing the advantages of investment diversification, this bill includes the 1990 budget proposal to allow pension funds to invest up to 20 per cent of their assets in foreign property by 1994.
The final 1990 budget measure forming part of Bill C-18 is a refinement of the rules relating to registered education savings plans. Changes will limit the total amount that may be contributed in respect of each beneficiary and will allow the payment of benefits to a beneficiary under a new plan only if he or she is a full-time student. Together with other related changes, these amendments will improve controls over the plans.
Other income tax measures included in Bill C-18 were announced in the budget introduced by the former Minister of Finance on February 26 of this year. These include special provisions for Canadians with disabilities and a modification of the taxation of gains on the shares of small business corporations.
In November 1990 the Minister of State Responsible for the Status of Disabled Persons announced a broad government strategy to promote equal opportunities for Canadians with disabilities. A number of measures in Bill C-18 bring that strategy to bear on the income tax system. First, the disability tax credit will be increased for 1991 from $575 to $700. This will increase federal assistance to disabled Canadians by $35 million a year. As well, the existing criteria for eligibility for the credit will be codified to ensure fair and uniform application.
The medical expense tax credit will also be enhanced by allowing non-working Canadians with disabilities to receive a credit for part-time attendant care and by expanding the list of medical expenses eligible for credit.
The cost of building renovations made to improve access for those with a disability will be deductible by the building owner immediately, rather than over a number of years. Many small businesses have complained to the government in this area and I think this is a major improvement for small businesses and for others to modify their buildings to assure that there is accessibility for those who have disabilities. This, of course, will help them immensely.
Where an employer provides transportation or related benefits to a blind employee or one whose mobility is
impaired, or provides an attendant to help a disabled employee perform his or her work, those benefits will not be included in the employee's income. That is another great advantage that we are placing in this bill.
Last, an individual receiving Canada or Quebec Pension Plan disability benefits in a lump sum will effectively be able to have those benefits taxed in the years in which they relate, rather than have the entire amount taxed in the year that it is received.

As I have said, these measures improve the ways in which the tax system delivers benefits to a group of Canadians most in need-those with physical or mental disabilities.

Another 1991 budget item included in Bill C-18 relates to the tax treatment of small business shareholding. An individual who realizes a capital gain on the disposition of shares of a qualifying small business corporation is eligible for an enhanced capital gains exemption of $500,000. Where a successful private corporation wants to expand, however, and does so by having its shares listed on a prescribed stock exchange in Canada, it will cease to be a qualifying small business corporation.
The enhanced exemption will then be unavailable to the original shareholders, even in respect of gains which accrued while the corporation did quality. Penalizing successful businesses in this way is counterproductive.
In order to allow a corporation to go public without sacrificing its shareholders' enhanced exemption, Bill C-18 will permit an individual to realize some or all of the latent capital gains on the shares without having actually to dispose of them. This measure is in keeping with the federal government's recognition of the pivotal economic role played by small business.
In addition to the income tax measures announced in the 1990 and 1991 budgets, Bill C-18 includes a number of provisions announced separately. Some of these are essentially technical in nature while others present significant tax initiatives. There are, for example, new rules relating to national labour-sponsored venture

capital corporations. These will encourage investment in small and developing businesses.
Other important amendments revise the system of tax benefits for residents of Canada's northern and isolated regions, simplify the computation of the investment income tax paid by life insurance companies, and implement what are known as the available-for-use rules for the timing of certain expenses and credits.
The government's commitment to culture and the arts, which I mentioned in describing the new rules for gifts of cultural property, is also reflected in measures included in this bill specifically to benefit artists. Employed artists will be able to claim a deduction for expenses incurred in the exercise of their artistic employment. A self-employed artist who donates certified works to designated institutions or public authorities will be entitled to claim a charitable tax credit without having the value of those works included in income. This is all part of the package of the federal government recognizing the importance of the artist to Canadian culture.
Bill C-18 also includes the package of provisions recently released by the Minister of National Revenue and designed to enhance administration fairness. These provisions give the minister discretion in a number of key areas. For example, the minister will be able to adjust the amount of tax payable and refund any overpayment should a taxpayer discover after the expiry of the normal reassessment period that he or she inadvertently had failed to claim a deduction.
The minister will also be able to waive penalties and interest where an individual has failed to comply with the law because of extraordinary circumstances such as a natural disaster or serious illness. I have run into these problems in my riding with small businesses. I am sure every member of the House has. These measures add significantly to the flexibility and responsiveness of the income tax system.
The final category of provisions included in Bill C-18 consists of a large number of what I call technical amendments. Many of these provide relief for taxpayers in unanticipated situations where the existing law would operate inappropriately. Other provisions ensure the internal consistency of the tax system or clarify ambiguous provisions. A few correct anomalies that unduly
Government Orders
favour certain taxpayers and a few reflect minor policy changes. Almost all of the technical amendments formed part of draft legislation released by the government in July 1990 and again in a revised version in February of this year.
The current legislation is, as I noted at the outset of my remarks, the product of extensive consultations with taxpayers and their advisers over that period.
I will not describe the technical amendments in any detail. Instead I refer hon. members to the explanatory notes prepared by the Department of Finance. These describe the entire bill clause by clause in ordinary, or at least relatively ordinary, language, as ordinary as they can get.
In summary, Bill C-18 both legislates a number of important tax measures already announced by the government and improves the income tax system in many technical respects. As a clear expression of the government's concern for the system's fairness and efficiency, this bill deserves the support of the House.
While I am on my feet, Mr. Speaker, may I move:
That Bill C-18, an act to amend the Income Ihx Act, the Canada Pension Plan, the Cultural Property Export and Import Act, the Income Tax Conventions Interpretation Act, the Thx Court of Canada Act, the Unemployment Insurance Act, the Canada-Newfoundland Atlantic Accord Implementation Act, the Canada Nova Scotia Offshore Petroleum Resources Accord Implementation Act, and certain related acts not to be referred to Legislative Committee Ebut be referred after second reading to the Standing Committee on Finance.
