speechtext: that Bill C-18, an act to amend the Income Tax Act, the Canada Pension Plan, the Cultural Property Export and Import Act, the Income Tax Conventions Interpretation Act, the Tax Court of Canada Act, the Unemployment Insurance Act, the Canada-Newfoundland Atlantic Accord Implementation Act, the Canada-Nova Scotia Offshore Petroleum Resources Accord Implementation Act and certain related acts, be read the second time and referred to Legislative Committee E.

Mr. Speaker, Bill C-18 is daunting in appearance. It has the appearance of a telephone book in thickness and contains a great many measures which can only be properly considered in committee. A lot of these measures are housekeeping or technical amendments to the tax system as it stands. In that respect, our over-all approach on this side of the House is to oppose the bill because it is part and parcel of a tax system which over all we oppose.
There are some good things in the bill. There are some measures in the bill which we would want to highlight as things that should have been done some time ago and
Government Orders
which are now finally being done and there are things in the bill which are particularly odious. I hope I might also have time to highlight them.
I wanted first of all to respond to some of the comments made by the member for Ottawa South who was speaking on behalf of the Liberal Party on Bill C-18.
There were some things the hon. member for Ottawa South had to say that I feel very supportive of, and I hope I get a chance to speak to them as well. But the one thing that struck me about what the member for Ottawa South had to say was the way in which he managed to talk about the unfairness of the tax system as it stands, without fessing up to the fact that much of the unfairness in the existing tax system owes its origins to the tax policies of many previous Liberal governments.
I am speaking, of course, Mr. Speaker, of the way in which many tax expenditures, which is the technical name if you like for what people on the street generally call tax loopholes, have their origins in the Liberal government policies of the 1970s and early 1980s. For instance, the member made mention of the dividend tax credit, and I am glad that he did. In that respect at least there has been a change in policy with the elimination of the manufacturing tax that permits the member for Ottawa South to argue for a change in the dividend tax credit without actually going back on Liberal policy. What the hon. member did not go into, as I have said before, was the way in which many of the tax expenditures have their origins in the tax expenditure policies of previous Liberal governments. These expenditures, we believe in this corner of the House, are at the root of the deficit and, therefore, at the root of the willingness on the part of this government to tax the middle class to death in order to help pay that deficit. It is not just the NDP that is saying that, Mr. Speaker, although that would be enough. The fact of the matter is that Statistics Canada in a recent study showed that some 44 per cent of the deficit, I believe, was attributable to tax expenditure policies, that is to say taxes which are not being collected and which could be and should be collected in many ways. Only 6 per cent is attributable to social spending and the other 50 per cent is attributable to the high interest rate policy of this government and the way in which that impacts on the deficit.

Government Orders
What we have here in this bill insofar as it is part of the over-all tax system is a tax system which reflects the values that were so clearly and exuberantly expressed on the night of the first budget of the Progressive Conservative government. I see the hon. member for Beaches- Woodbine there. He will remember that day when the first time that Michael Wilson, the member for Etobicoke Centre, presented a budget, the thing that brought the entire Conservative caucus to its feet in a standing ovation unlike any I have seen here before, was the announcement of the $500,000 lifetime capital gains exemption. It was at that time that I realized the tremendous gulf that existed between me and my constituents, and the government and its supporters-the gulf I might say, Mr. Speaker, that exists in the biblical story between Dives and Lazarus. The great gulf between the rich man Dives and Lazarus the poor man at the gate, which can never be crossed it seems.
I asked myself, Mr. Speaker, who in my constituency was rising in their livingrooms to celebrate this $500,000 lifetime capital gains exemption? The answer, of course, is no one.
This was an exemption that was thought to be the pinnacle of Tory financial policy, which was completely irrelevant to the financial needs of the people in a constituency like Winnipeg-Transcona, with the possible exception maybe of a handful of people who do not make themselves known to me.
The fact of the matter is that we have had financial, fiscal, and taxation policies which have been directed, quite openly and honestly and straightforwardly on the part of the government, to making the rich richer in this country. The Minister of Finance said it himself. He said there are not enough rich people in Canada. Well, he has been true to his own perception of the problem, he has been helping the rich to get richer, as the hon. member for Ottawa South said. He was recounting some very familiar statistics that it is the people in the very top income brackets of the Canadian population who have benefited most from what has been called, in a bastardization of the concept, "tax reform" by this government.
This has not been tax reform in any sense of the word, in any sense of the way in which ordinary Canadians mean it when they call for tax reform. When they call for
tax reform what they mean is that the tax system ought to become more fair, that the tax system ought to require more of those who can afford it and less of those who cannot. Instead, we have a tax system which, admittedly, has provided some breaks to lower income people but at the same time has provided enormous relief to people in the very high income brackets. The people who are feeling it the most, who are really taking it in the teeth, so to speak, are the middle income people.
I think that we are approaching a point in the life of Canadian politics where the middle class is saying: "We can't take it any more." The GST was the final straw. The people who cannot take it any more, and who cannot take it any the most, and this is where I agree with the member for Ottawa South, are in many cases, middle class families with children. The member went into a great deal of detail because he had a lot more time than I will have to go into the discrepancies and inequities which exist within the tax system with respect to people who have children, and how people who are middle class are not receiving the kind of support for raising children that they used to receive as a result of the tax system, as a result of the clawback on family allowances, and as a result of the way in which our school system and various other things are becoming almost user fee places.
I am constantly surprised in my own situation at the things that my kids come back from school and say: "We have to buy this, we have to buy that, we have to buy this, and we have to buy that." I remember in the 1940s, 1950s and 1960s, this was the kind of thing that the school supplied.
I think what is happening in the tax system is that increasingly for middle and upper income people, children are not being regarded as something which all of society has a responsibility to help parents support. Children are being regarded as sort of consumer choices that middle and upper income people are making and it is up to them to support their own consumer choices. If some other couple decides not to have any children and spend their money on winter holidays instead of raising children, well, we live in a free society and we all make choices.
I do not see it that way. I think that there ought to be more support for people who are raising children regardless of the income. That is why we support the family

allowance system and it is why we oppose the clawback and the deindexing of family allowances.
The member also made mention of the way in which the tax system discriminates against marriage. Maybe I have a conflict of interest that I should declare because in my other vocation, as a United Church minister, I am in the habit of marrying people from time to time. I think marriage is a good thing, and I do not see why the tax system should discriminate against marriage in this way. I do not ask it to discriminate in favour of marriage. I simply ask, as the hon. member for Ottawa South asked, that it be neutral, at the very least, with respect to this kind of choice which faces many people.
Just those few words about what the hon. member for Ottawa South had to say. As far as Bill C-18 is concerned, there are as I said a great many things in it which concern us. Some of the things we think are worth highlighting on the positive side are that it gives an exception from the tighter rules on travel and work allowances for visually impaired people, or attendants for mentally and physically impaired people. In fact, some of the best elements of this bill have to do with changes with respect to disabled people, increasing the disability tax credit, for instance.
At the same time there are elements in the bill which give an indication that the government wants to tighten up eligibility for some of these benefits. It is a bit of giving with one hand and the taking with the other, and we would like to explore that more.
Nevertheless, these are some of the positive dimensions of the bill that we have before us. For instance, it closes a loophole on the capital cost allowance for cars. It extends a deduction with respect to encouraging firms to make buildings more accessible for the disabled, again a thing which will help to increase justice for the disabled in this country. It enables tuition payments for courses paid for unemployment insurance to be deducted from UI income.
Now, Mr. Speaker, you will be pleased to know that as a result of this bill it is now officially against the law to deduct the cost of bribing government officials as a cost of doing business.
Oh, oh.

This is a great ethical advancement in the income tax system.
Government Orders
The departmental officials maintain that this was not a widespread problem or anything, but there are some countries in which greasing the wheel is just the way to get things done. This is being put in so it cannot be claimed that its absence made it legal. This is a great step forward.
I will resist the temptation to respond to the heckling of my own colleagues here.
It extends a deduction to those receiving gallantry awards for war service. It extends medical exemptions and credits to incontinence products, mobility-aiding devices, animals which help humans, et cetera, and dwelling modifications. It also provides that no interest will be charged to the taxpayer if they receive an overpayment of their GST credit.
It allows for going back and more easily fixing mistakes and getting refunds. It raises the large corporation tax from .175 per cent to .2 per cent on capital over $10 million. This is a real hard-hitting measure. It goes a long way toward making the corporations pay their fair share. All we can say is that it is a step in the right direction, but they have got a long way to go before they will be asking the large corporations to actually be paying their way.
In the same way that this government gets tough with the corporations, sarcastically speaking, it introduces a new penalty for the large corporation tax late payments which is all of one-quarter of 1 per cent of the total per complete month, compared to roughly 5 per cent of the total amount plus 12 per cent per annum for individuals, another example of the great gap which exists between how this government treats individual Canadians and how it treats its friends in the corporate sector.
The one other good thing, I am told, in the bill is that in the language of the bill, there is exclusive language in the form of always referring to the taxpayer as he or his has been removed and we now have a language of referring to the taxpayer. I am glad to see that the government has finally caught on to the use of inclusive language and sought, when it has the opportunity, to eliminate the use of exclusive language in that way.
Some of the clauses that we would like to highlight because we find them to be ones that we would like to highlight for opposition have to do with loosening the rules on deduction for self-employed home office expenses which allow indefinite carryover of losses when

October 7, 1991
Government Orders
one's home expenses are more than the income earned from self-employment.
We also single out for opposition the fact that money which people receive through the Older Worker Adjustment Program will be taxable like UI income. It seems to me that workers who find themselves in this position as a result of a plant shutdown or whatever and find themselves eligible for the Older Worker Adjustment Program should get some kind of a tax break especially when we consider that capital gains are only taxed at 75 per cent. Why not some kind of exemption for people who find themselves in this very difficult situation?
I am pointing out the difference between the comprehensive way in which the government seeks to tax ordinary Canadians regardless of their circumstance and the breaks which exist on the corporate side.
There is also the question of northern tax benefit changes which the hon. member for Churchill will be speaking to in more detail on our behalf.
As I said before, the disability tax credit has increased from $575 to $700 per year. It is only indexed to inflation above 3 per cent per year. In other words, it is receiving the same kind of treatment that other social programs have. One wonders how the government came to the conclusion that the needs of the disabled only increase by the amount of inflation above 3 per cent if it is serious about actually helping people to meet those needs.
The bill also provides the minister more latitude in checking on whether people are disabled. He puts strict definitions on medical impairments for instance. Revenue Canada has already been cracking down and reassessing people back over the years for this one.
The definition of disabled is to be strictly drawn, but leaves a very wide open crack for people, especially the mentally handicapped to fall into. Whether one can work or keep up a house has been explicitly excluded, for instance, from determining disability. We think this is a matter of great concern.
The hon. member for Beaches-Woodbine has a history of being concerned about the rights of the disabled. He may have something say about this in the course of the debate, but I do not know.
I know my time is running out, but I have just a few more points.
The other thing this does is remove the transfer of education tax credits to relatives if the course is recreational in nature. We have heard a great deal on this from music teachers and particularly people who are in official schools of music. Not only have they been recently hit by the GST, which makes it much more difficult for parents to send their children for these kinds of music lessons, but removing this particular ability of the parents to have the tuition credits transferred to them is another difficulty which these music schools will find themselves in. Perhaps in committee we might be able to persuade the minister to consider something in this respect.
In any event, I see that I have no time left. This will no doubt bring great pleasure to my Liberal colleagues who do not like to hear me go on and on about how the tax system we have, in many respects, owes its unfairness to the Liberal party. I am sorry that I do not have more time to go into that. I know they are not. We will have time in the future.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Are there comments or questions? Resuming debate.
Before I recognize another member, it is my duty, pursuant to Standing Order 38, to inform the House that the questions to be raised tonight at the time of adjournment are as follows: the hon. member for York West- The Airline Industry; the hon. member for Willowdale-Employment; the hon. member for Drummond-Textile and Garment Industries; the hon. member for Vancouver East-Multiculturalism; and the hon. member for Algoma-Agriculture.
I now give the floor to the hon. member for York West. [English]

Mr. Speaker, let me tell my hon. friend from the New Democratic Party that Liberals are prepared to talk about taxes and any other issue and it would be nice if the provincial government of my own province would also engage in that fruitful debate from time to time.
I am pleased to rise in my place to speak on Bill C-18, an act to amend the Income Thx Act and other acts. This legislation was introduced on May 30 by the Minister of

Finance and proposes to change many of the tax provisions imposed on Canadians by this government.
Bill C-18 is an extensive piece of legislation. It will be noted that it encompasses some 400 pages, with over 250 clauses aimed at reforming our tax laws.
As the critic for transportation matters for my caucus and party, I am certainly pleased to leave much of the debate to our financial critics and other colleagues of the House. As the transport critic, I would rather raise and concentrate on one provision, one clause, that relates largely to the shipping industry in this country.
Speaking of shipping, it is no secret that the Canadian shipping industry has been badly hurt by some of the economic policies of the government. That is not to exclude other areas of the transport industry. We have been witness in this Chamber to similar complaints from the trucking industry. When the government deregulated the trucking industry in 1988 and opened up the floodgates for American truckers, we clearly know what the result was, much to the detriment of Canadian truckers and the Canadian trucking industry.
Similarly, we have seen the repeat exercise on the air side in terms of the open skies negotiations, whereby the Americans would want to compete freely and openly in Canada and also abroad and pick up passengers in this country. We will, I think, face the same type of results in the air side that unfortunately our truckers have met with if we allow those negotiations to take place and allow free trade in the sky.
Shipping certainly is not excluded in terms of the transportation infrastructure and the transportation network across the country. Ship owners, Canadian crews, seafarers, shipbuilders and our ports have all reeled from the disinterest of this government to respond to the current economic crisis and to manage the crisis in a much better fashion.
To a great extent the Tory made-in-Canada recession, the elimination of thousands of jobs, the government's disadvantaged tax laws, and excessive user fees, among other matters, have made the Canadian shipping industry uncompetitive through no fault of its own.
Government Orders
As those involved will know, international shipping is largely and exclusively a foreign controlled industry. Canadian shippers have often reflagged their vessels to take advantage of foreign laws, different employment practices and more competitive markets.
The provisions of clause 194 in Bill C-18 which affect our shipping industry aim to put our shippers on a more equal footing with our international competition by allowing shippers with foreign incorporation to not pay taxes on profits generated from exclusively international operations.
Having said that, I think this particular clause is on the right course with respect to righting this wrong. Specifically, the bill would add a new provision to the Income Tax Act to determine that when a corporation's principal operating residence is incorporated outside Canada for the purposes of transporting goods and/or passengers, its profits generated from international shipping opportunities would not be taxable here in Canada and thus would try to correct what has been over a number of years a discouraging variable, if you will, of not having companies register in Canada because the fear was that once you registered in Canada, not only the Canadian routes would be taxed, but all your international shipping business and transactions would become taxable.
What you have happening in Canada is very few foreign firms incorporating in Canada and also driving many of our own shipping companies to reflag in different parts of the world, such as Bermuda. The net effect was that the economic activity and the economic spinoffs were not taking place in Canada, but in other ports across the world.
It should be noted also that under the scope of the legislation departure or destination points on the St. Lawrence or the Great Lakes would not constitute international shipping as a protection to the businesses enjoyed by Canadians currently.
Currently, corporations in Canada pay tax on their world-wide income, as I mentioned moments ago, if they are a principal resident of Canada and if they are incorporated here. Such a fiscal provision has not been conducive to international shipping and many Canadian shipping companies have been hurt by a policy which curtails exclusively international business opportunities.

October 7, 1991
Government Orders
International shipping is truly an operation which depends on world-wide support. Often the crews, the seamen, the financing, the ship's construction, the ownership, cargo, management, chartering and the operations of one ship are from many separate countries.
An example of such internationalism was brought to my attention from an article in Maclean's magazine last year. In it the writer mentioned an example pertaining to an international vessel which carried British Columbian coal to Japanese steel mills. The ship was built in South Korea, financed by an American bank with Asian dollars, registered in Liberia, owned by Panamanians, with shares insured in London. The ship was subsequently chartered in Bermuda, managed in Hong Kong with staff from India and crewed by British officers and Filipino seamen.
That illustrates the complexities which have become the reality in this particular industry. As a shipping nation Canada must become competitive with the other world giants. Regrettably to date the policies of this government have inhibited the opportunities of our international shipping companies, the Canadian crews and our Canadian shipbuilders. For instance, when we talked about the United States of America, they were very ready to open up the trucking industry and push for it, and we gave in. They were very willing to open up the air market, and we are on the verge of allowing them to do that. When it came to shipping, where our vessels in fact can compete head to head with the Americans, they hide behind the Jones Act and refuse to talk about the shipping industry.
That is an example of the fallacy of the argument that this government has pursued, that where we are strong, and where we can compete, we are very hesitant to open up that market, yet where we go into it no holds barred, such as the trucking and the air side, because economies of scales dictate, we are getting hurt as a result.
In 1988, according to Statistics Canada, Canadian international shipping reach 250 million tonnes. Evidently, we are a trading nation, and a shipping nation, but under this government we have not become a competitive nation in this regard.
Allowing, therefore, Canadian shipping companies to take advantage of the international shipping opportunities I think is a pursuit that we ought to pursue as a
House and as a country. Canadian shipping companies have long understood that they are willing to pay their fair share of the tax burden in Canada for their operations domestically. Even the Seafarers' International Union can see that the provisions to exempt exclusive foreign operations is a step in the right direction.
On the one extreme, I think the economic opportunities certainly can be fulfilled. For example, an umbrella organization, an advisory council called the Asia-Pacific Initiative, has recently lobbied the government and other members of Parliament with the belief that such an amendment in this bill would in fact increase the opportunities and the economic spin-offs. For instance, they have quoted that in the Vancouver area alone, if we were to set up and establish an international shipping corporation, it would create as a result 1,600 new jobs over a three year period. As well, it would infuse the local regional economy with $1 billion, and $180 million in purchases of local goods and services.
They feel that there would be a fleet of some 200 ships that would be owned, managed and controlled out of Canada's Pacific coastal waters, rather than the current 12 which are currently in production. I think we in fact can obtain and incur a number of economic spin-offs that are now going to other countries because of the tax regime that we have in place in Canada.
At the same time, however, a number of questions should be answered by the Minister of Finance before the debate concludes. Clearly the opportune moment is not only on second reading, as we are engaging in now, but clearly to seek some clarification and answers at the committee stage by my hon. colleagues who sit on the finance committee.
First, I would like to raise and question the beneficial impact of the proposed legislation as it pertains to the particular shipping clause in Bill C-18 on the employment of Canadian crews. Will, for example, the provisions of clause 194 mean lost jobs for Canadian seafarers? Will this legislation employ thousands of foreign ship workers and displace those Canadians trying to earn a living, and an income, on Canadian ships? What will happen to the opportunities abroad for our Canadian crews and will some of the international shipping lines also engage in more local competition with existing Canadian firms?
October 7, 1991

Insofar as some of those questions go, Mr. Andrew Boyle, Secretary-Treasurer of the Seafarers' International Union of Canada, wrote a letter on April 3 of this year to the hon. Minister of Finance to try to clarify some of these similar points. I would like to quote a paragraph from his letter which I think touches on the problem at hand. He states: "While it is a step in the right direction to put Canadian marine interests on an equal footing with their foreign competitors, any net benefit that would arise by this amendment would be inconsequential versus the thousands of job losses that have and will result from the government-encouraged reflagging of Canadian ships."
He goes on to say: "With thousands of Canadians depending on the marine industry for their livelihood, and in light of the federal government's continued marine policies that discriminate against Canadians and enhance opportunities of growth for Canadian multinationals and foreign shipping fleets, and the thousands of jobs that go with them, we hereby respectfully request that you review the attached proposal concerning Canadian seafarers working on board ship and trading internationally."
I think the Seafarers' International Union has certainly been a large voice, an important voice, and a realistic voice when it comes to the shipping industry. It would be my hope that the committee at committee stage would take a hard look at some of the concerns that not only he but other members of the shipping industry have raised in response to Bill C-18.
I hope that these concerns as well as others that have been mentioned by my hon. colleague, the hon. member for Ottawa South, will be listened to. I know that certainly my colleague from Hamilton Mountain will be talking about other concerns as they relate to other constituencies.
I would love to get into the details of the other facets of the shipping industry, but I am going to refrain from doing so. I know that Bill C-33, a shipping bill, will be coming up for debate in the House of Commons in a matter of days, and I will try to save some of the larger general issues for the debate that will ensue on Bill C-33.
Government Orders
What I had wanted to do this afternoon in a short span of time is try to raise this one particular clause of many in Bill C-18 that relates to the shipping industry. I think it provides both an opportunity in terms of amending our laws to bring greater economic activity to our Canadian ports, to our shipping industry, and also to realize some of the other options and multiplier effects that can bring greater economic wealth at a time when this country so desperately needs it.
At the same time we are going to engage in seizing an economic opportunity, I think we have to be fully cognizant and sensitive to some of the concerns that have been raised by the Seafarers' because in our rush and in our pursuit perhaps to change and amend our laws, we also may be watching and incurring a down side in other areas.
Certainly protection of jobs by the Canadian Seafarers' and Canadians engaged right now is obviously very high on the national agenda, as so it should be. I believe if we are sensible and if we are cognizant of those concerns we can realize the economic benefit of amending our tax laws and at the same time protect and encourage our Canadian jobs and Canadian crews to ensure that our shipping industry is put once again on a stronger foundation so that it may compete with the world's best.

Mr. Speaker, according to the government, its current strategy for the disabled consists of two main elements.
First, the income tax amendments contained in the legislation that we are debating today, Bill C-18. Second, the national strategy for disabled persons announced by the Prime Minister in Winnipeg a few weeks ago.
If those were in fact the principle elements of the government's strategy for persons with disability, I would be prepared to stand in the House of Commons and commend the government for taking some reasonable first steps in assisting Canada's disabled citizens.
The sad fact is, however, that the government's overall strategy for disabled persons is not deserving of praise. It is deserving of manifest condemnation.
Conservative members of Parliament point with pride to amendments in Bill C-18 and say: "We are giving disabled persons $65 million". Those same Conservatives seem to forget that one week ago, they voted for

October 7, 1991
Government Orders
Bill C-32, which will remove more than $2 billion from the Canada Assistance Plan payments.
They voted for a measure which will cut home care for disabled persons, which will cut health care for disabled persons, which will cut rehabilitation programs for disabled persons, which will cut programs for independent living for disabled persons and which will cut employment service for disabled persons.
Conservative members of Parliament also point with pride to the Prime Minister's announcement in Winnipeg of $31 million in programs for disabled persons. These same Conservatives seem to forget that a year ago they voted for Bill C-69 which slashed social service funding by billions of dollars, which slashed establishment programs financing by billions of dollars. These same Conservatives seem to forget that they voted to cut the Canada Jobs Strategy fund by $100 million, that they voted to cut social housing by $411 million, that they voted to reduce cash transfers to the provinces for medicare. The Conservative government has cut social programs by billions upon billions of dollars.
Those programs are the very ones which disabled citizens rely upon to help them get proper medical care, to help them receive training, to help them obtain proper accommodation, to help them get out of poverty, to help them live in with a maximum degree of dignity and a maximum degree of freedom.
The government has undermined all of the major programs which disabled Canadians need in order to succeed. In return the government now offers disabled Canadians the $65 million of tax changes contained in Bill C-18 and the $31 million a year more in benefits promised by the Prime Minister.
When one considers there are 3.3 million disabled Canadians, then one will see that the changes offered in Bill C-18 work out to an average of less than $20 per year for every disabled Canadian. That is less than $1.60 a month, about a nickel a day.
Using the same simple arithmetic, the Prime Minister's promise of new programs works out to 90 cents a month, less than 3 cents a day for every disabled Canadian.
Shame.

In short, the government has acted to decimate the health, educational, rehabilitation, housing and social assistance services which are critical to disabled Canadians and in exchange for committing that outrage the government is offering every disabled Canadian tax breaks and new services which work out to 8 cents a day for each one of them.
That, Mr. Speaker, is a national disgrace.
In his budget which led to the legislation we are discussing in the House of Commons today, the Minister of Finance had the nerve to say this government has done more than any other to improve opportunities and to enable Canadians with disabilities to participate more fully and more fairly in the work place, in their communities and at home.
Contrast those words of the Minister of Finance with the words used by the Canadian Cerebral Palsy Association when commenting on the government's legislation to cut back Canada Assistance Plan funding: "The extraordinary suffering which it imposes on poor and disabled Canadians cannot be justified."
There are 552,000 visually impaired Canadians. That means that even with glasses those Canadians have difficulty reading normal print. There are 46,625 legally blind Canadians. These Canadians, our fellow citizens, need the programs which this Conservative government has cut back. Forty-four per cent of Canadians with a disability have eight or fewer years of schooling. These disabled Canadians need more help, not less.
As appalling as those numbers are, they are not nearly as appalling, not nearly as distressing as some other numbers I would like to put on the record.
According to the most recent statistics officially known as the Health and Activity Limitations Survey, these are the number of disabled Canadians living in poverty:
195,000	Canadians with hearing impairment live in poverty, 225,000 Canadians with mental disabilities live in poverty, 134,000 Canadians with visual impairment live in poverty, 493,000 Canadians with mobility impairment live in poverty, 407,000 Canadians with agility impairment live in poverty.
Let me point out that agility impairment is a technical way of saying limited ability to dress or undress, get in and out of bed, cut your toenails or use your fingers.
October 7, 1991

I ask you, in 1991 in Canada what are 407,000 Canadians with agility impairment doing living in poverty? What are one-third of disabled Canadians between the ages of 15 and 24 doing living in poverty? What are 29.5 per cent of disabled women doing living in poverty?
Massive issues are confronting all of us in providing proper and fair legislation for Canadians with disabilities. There are the issues of financial security, employment opportunities and employment equity, independent and community living, promotion of disabled rights and the prevention of disabilities.
I do not expect Bill C-18 to solve all the problems but I do expect the government to be honest. This legislation which the government hails as a major step forward in the tax treatment of disabled Canadians is, in fact, a mere drop in the bucket, and it is a mere drop in the bucket which has just been emptied by this government. Whatever measures are contained in this bill come nowhere close to compensating disabled Canadians for the losses they are suffering from government cutbacks in other legislation.
As my colleague the hon. member for Ottawa South has already indicated, we in the Official Opposition are prepared to see this bill proceed to a legislative committee in fairly short order for detailed study. I appreciate that the legislative committee will have its work cut out for it, and I would not presume to suggest to the committee every possible area of the bill it may wish to examine. There are, however, some thoughts which I hope the legislative committee will keep in mind when studying those aspects of Bill C-18 which affect Canadians with disabilities.
Clause 90 of the bill sets out the government's proposal for disability tax credit. I hope the committee will realize that nearly three million disabled Canadians will receive no benefit from the disability tax credit. This is the largest specific budgetary item offered to disabled Canadians, and yet 90 per cent of them are ineligible to claim it. I hope the committee will keep that in mind when suggesting improvements to the bill.
Clause 91 of the bill will put into the Income Tax Act specific legal definitions for those who are eligible to receive the disability tax credit. At present those definitions are handled by regulation. I would hope that the
Government Orders
committee will consider whether it is wise to make this change from regulation to statute. Do we run the risk of excluding certain people from receiving the credit? Is the certainty of a statute better than the flexibility of regulations?
Committee members will also want to allay the concerns of some disability rights advocates as to whether the disability tax credit and the medical expenses tax credit are complementary. Does the legislation guarantee with absolute certainty that disabled Canadians can claim one benefit without risk of losing the other?
I would hope that with respect to the medical expenses tax credit that the legislative committee will revisit the decision to limit tax assistance for part-time attendant care expenses to expenses incurred in respect of an attendant who is not a relative of a disabled person. Is there a sound reason for this limitation? Does this limitation not run the risk of discriminating against disabled Canadians living in rural or isolated areas where the only person who could possibly serve as an attendant might well be a relative?
Clause 15 of the bill deals with deductibility of business expenses incurred in modifying premises to accommodate disabled persons. In a technical vein, we in the opposition are concerned that this provision appears narrowly defined to limit the deduction to businesses providing greater access only for those with mobility impairment. Does this rule out a deduction for such innovations as talking elevators or visual fire alarms? If so, we hope the bill will be amended.
In a broader vein, it is worth while to note that the government has failed to place a price tag on this provision of the bill. Is that because the government realizes that this measure is simply not enough of an incentive to businesses to modify their premises? Is there a smarter way, a more effective way, of encouraging businesses to modify their premises to provide access for disabled persons? I hope the committee will consider that.
There are then a number of technical issues which must be considered with regard to the impact of this bill upon disabled Canadians. But I want to be clear; it is not this bill per se which troubled me, indeed within its own narrow context this bill contains certain proposals which will prove of some value to some disabled Canadians.

October 7, 1991
Government Orders
What troubles me is that the government believes this bill addresses in a serious manner the range of problems facing disabled Canadians. What troubles me more is that other actions by the government negate many, many times over any of the positive benefits which this bill may provide.
As my party's spokesman for disabled persons, I was pleased to be able to arrange a series of hearings across Canada this summer with disabled individuals and with groups representing disabled persons. I want to thank my many colleagues in the Liberal caucus who took part in these meetings. We gleaned a large number of excellent suggestions. We heard from a host of people who have never previously had an opportunity to present their ideas to members of Parliament. We will use these ideas in the months ahead as we press for a fairer deal for disabled Canadians.
I only wish that every member of Parliament on the government side had the same opportunity because I am certain that they would reverse the unfair and unwise strategy which they have undertaken. They would see the foolishness in cutting back on health care for disabled persons. They would see the foolishness in cutting back on housing for disabled persons. They would see the foolishness in cutting back on rehabilitation services for disabled Canadians. They would see the foolishness in cutting back on training programs for disabled persons. They would see the foolishness in cutting back on job programs for disabled persons.
All that individual Canadians with disabilities are asking for is the same as the rest of us want. All that individual Canadians with disabilities are asking for is the opportunity to reach their maximum potential. Surely, as a society, that is what we want. Surely, in 1991, it is not too much for any Canadian to ask. I urge the government, I plead with the government, to give Canadians with disabilities that chance.

Mr. Speaker, I want to participate in this debate because this is an important issue for Canadians. I cannot think of anything that is more important to most Canadians than income tax. I think in most kitchens and places where people gather this is the kind of matter they are talking about, perhaps more than the Constitution, perhaps more even than the
popularity of the current Prime Minister. Every day now, people are getting concerned about taxes of different kinds.
I cannot think of a matter that requires more attention from my staff and myself as we try to respond to telephone calls and letters. People are becoming attuned to the tax system. People are asking me interesting questions about income tax, the goods and services tax, the provincial sales taxes, when they pay them and when they do not pay them, and they are beginning to understand some of the complexities of it all. They are beginning to understand how to buy muffins so that no tax is paid on them. They are beginning to go into stores and argue that maybe the banner in the store that says: "We absorb the GST", does not really do any good when they pay the provincial sales tax on top of the price of the goods and a so-called absorbed GST. People are beginning to have some sense of the nuances.
One of the things that disturbs me about this bill is that it is basically a continuation and an expansion of the nuances of the whole income tax system.
I think we should start with the name of the bill because I would defy any of the Ministers of the Crown and any of the half dozen or so members who are here this afternoon to be able to just kind of flip this one off your lips. It is just not possible to do that. Here is the size of the bill. Most towns in Canada do not have a phone book this size and this is not the whole package, this is a partial package. This is the beginning of the latest round of shuffling of the deck.
I think that Canadians, as a group, have a legitimate beef when they say this to people like me. They want to know why, when they sign a contract with the Canadian Tire store, with Woolco, with K-Mart and with any other business with whom they might come in contact, the laws of Canada, Ontario and most of our provinces say that when you draw up a sales agreement, the consumer has some rights and one of the rights is the very simple right of being able to understand what they are being charged and what the process is. If somebody came into a member's office and said: "Listen, I got this bill in the mail and it says I signed a contract. I tried to read this thing, but I do not understand it. Do I have to get a lawyer to interpret this contract?"

Most of us would say well, wait a minute, there is probably a law somewhere on the books provincially or federally which says the consumer has a right to a reasonable amount of knowledge and the obligation is on people in the private sector to explain in reasonable language the service they are providing. And so the day, supposedly, of being able to write up a contract that no one can understand except your lawyer and thereby disabusing the public in some way is long gone.
I defy anybody, any ordinary Canadian, to pick up an income tax form and tell me what the hell it is all about. It cannot be done. I am one of those who was pleased last year when a short form was put out, a short form that was intended to allow people to fill out their income tax a little faster and be a little more convenient for the public.
Well I got the short form. I have been reading short forms like this for about 30 years. I did not understand it. We had to have family conferences about what this short form meant. When we compared the short form to the longer form, we found out in our family that in order to get to use this shorter form, we had to forgo several privileges that had been previously extended to us in the income tax system.
Maybe we should put a stamp on the outside of the short form that says you can use this form, but it is going to cost you money. If you want to use the short form you have to pay more income tax this year. Danger. Warning. Just like on a pack of cigarettes. If you fill out this form it is going to be dangerous to your pocketbook. That would be fair for the consumer, but it did not say that. Instead it purported to be something that would simplify paying your taxes to the Government of Canada.
Reading through this bill is a challenge which I doubt most Canadians will take. As a matter of fact, I doubt that most members of this House will read it either. But if you read this bill, it is a confusing array of reality. It is kind of a bureaucrat's portrayal of what is going on here.
I want to read into the record just one section because I think some of this is pretty interesting. Subsection 28. Follow this if you can, and determine for me, Mr. Speaker, whether it is English, French or something else.
Subsection 10 is applicable after June 17, 1987 except that that
portion of the definition small business corporation in subsection
Government Orders
248(1) of the said act, preceding paragraph (a) thereof as enacted by subsection 10 shall, after June 17, 1987 and before September 14, 1988 be read as follows:
Would you repeat that?

What does it mean? In which of our official languages was that written? Is it conceivable that the Canadian public could understand that? I know that someone will explain to a poor soul like me that this is not meant to be read by the public, it is meant to be read by lawyers, it is meant to be read by tax accountants, it is meant to be read by bureaucrats.
Most of us who have been members for a little while can tell some little anecdote about someone who came to their office last week and you tried to explain, as I have done on several occasions now, why it is that the Government of Canada is suggesting to people that he or she really does not want to be married. You want to be divorced because if you get divorced, you fall into this definition of this regulation in this act, and therefore there is a financial advantage to you.
Surely that is not our business, and yet that is the way this bill is written, and that is the way most acts that have to do with income tax are written. It is the definition.
Try to explain to somebody who is trying to earn a living as a commercial fisherman why it is so difficult for them, and yet so attractive for someone who wants to set up a charter fishing company as a tax loss. That is a confusing thing to try to do, and it is a hurtful thing to try to do. Surely that was not the intention of the Income Tkx Act in the first instance.
I am constantly reminded that income tax was supposedly a temporary tax. Hardly. If you go through the provisions that are in this bill, one almost despairs that there is any sense of fairness left in the approach to it all. I understand, as somebody who has been in politics for a little while, that the income tax provisions in a very broad sense are used as the levers of a government to encourage some things to happen, to discourage other things. Perhaps what needs to be done is at some point in time you need to take all of those incentives and kind of hive them off in some other way, because caught in the middle of this is the ordinary person who has the pay cheque. They are the poor, unfortunate souls who are the victims of this process. They are the ones that cannot afford to play the game, and so they do not have a great

Government Orders
many investments. They do not have any money left in their take home pay to do any investing.
They are the victims in the sense that they are dependent on other people to interpret simple tax forms so they can fulfil their obligations under the law. An interesting test would be, and I cannot think of a similar circumstance, to see how fair it would be if there were other laws that people just simply could not interpret, could not function on the signs of the law.
In the Highway Traffic Act, for example, if all the signs were posted in the jargon that income tax laws are written in, it would be interesting to see what would happen as everybody went up to the stop sign, ran out and had to get a lawyer to interpret whether the sign said stop or go, whether the light was green or red, to seek professional advice to follow the letter of the law. We all say that is nuts. In effect, that is exactly what this approach to income tax causes all Canadians to do.
I want to get back to something I said a little earlier about the bitterness out there about the process. I am not sure that Canadians ever want to understand this bill or the income tax process entirely. Most of them do not care. Quite frankly, that is not why they are living their lives. That is not the purpose that motivates them every day. It is something that is now beginning to impede them and they are beginning to become increasingly aware that they are victims in this process, that this is not designed to be a fair process. This is a process which mitigates against them and their families and prevents them from accomplishing very much in economic terms during their working lifetimes. They are now beginning to understand that at the end of their working lifetimes, it continues to work against them, it hits them when they retire and it hurts them where it hurts the most, in their pocketbooks. When they try to provide for themselves and their families, they know they are working in an income tax system that is written against their best interests.
It is also true that it is written in the best interests of a veiy small percentage of the population, those who have the ability to compete in this kind of a field, those who have the ability to hire the lawyers and use the tax accountants and to use them well and to use them every single day.
Most people I know who are in business now would probably count their tax advisers among the most important people in their whole business organization, not the people who actually make things, not the people who actually dream up things, not the people who are productive. The people who are critical to the operation very often turn out to be their tax advisers. That is the critical point on whether somebody can stay in business. That is the critical point on whether a product line can expand. Was that the intention? I do not think it was. I think that a long time ago we had a very different concept of what an income tax process was all about.
The bitterness in Canadian people is beginning to manifest itself in some rather unfortunate ways, and I do not think anybody would deny this. More and more people I know are consciously working to find a way out of the whole income tax process entirely.
This summer at my home in Oshawa, I had a string of people banging on my door offering me one price if I wanted to pay by cheque or by credit card, and quite a different price if I wanted to pay by cash. There was a little wink and a nudge attached to that. There was no doubt in my mind that what was going on here is that the guy who wanted to coat my driveway with some kind of sealant had figured it out to the extent that if there were paperwork involved, there was income tax involved. If the paperwork involved me putting some green money into his hand, there was no income tax involved and from his personal perspective that was better than running a legitimate business that might be taxed at some point in time.
I think Canadian people are beginning to sense that the system is wrong. It is not a fair system. It is not one which tries to differentiate between the rich and poor, except that the rich have an ability to utilize the system better than the poor. Caught in the middle are all those people who work for a living, all those who take home a pay cheque.
We had a little debate in here this morning. It was unfortunate, because I thought it was a good idea for a Private Members' Bill to say to seniors: "Here is an answer for you. It may be to your advantage to pay your income tax once a year, rather than quarterly". The government had no time for this kind of concern.
There are a lot of people who are now just beginning to think: "Wait a minute. If somebody else on my block can avoid paying income tax, how did they do that". Maybe if I had an ability to hang on to my tax money for most of the year instead of giving it to the government
October 7, 1991

earlier on in the year I could use my money to pay my debts instead of giving it to the federal government.
They are beginning to understand simple things like this: So what if there is a tax credit involved? So what if there is some kind of a rebate involved? First I have to pay the tax and then wait six months, eight months, nine months, twelve months, for some government agency to send me out a cheque. They are beginning to figure out that there is a disadvantage in that for them, that the cheque never seems to quite match their original expenditure and even if it does, they have to give somebody the money for a year and then wait to get it back.
That is not a fair system. The problem with all of this, aside from just the wrong-headedness of it all, is that this is an income tax system which cannot work in this country. I have heard other members say this before me so it is not a revelation and it is not a view which I alone hold. This is a tax system which is based on the simple notion that it is fair enough that the people will pay without having to do a whole lot of auditing or chasing after people. They will see it as a fair system, they will see it essentially as one in which they are paying their fair share. The moment people see it as something other than that, if they see it as a system which cheats them, they are going to try to cheat the system. They are going to tiy to cheat back. One can hardly blame them for that because they see examples of it all around them.
They see corporations which operate within the letter of the law, one should not be accusing the corporations of breaking laws here, with the advantage of having a resource of tax advisers who tell them how to work that law, who tell them how to delay the payment of taxes, who tell them how to avoid the payment of taxes, who tell them how to borrow money so they can write it down, and who tell them what to write off and what to not and to what extent.
When ordinary citizens take a look at that, they say "wait a minute, maybe I had better find some of this information out, maybe I had better start to use some of this information too". I believe that moment has already set in. I guess the basic thing is, to go back to something I stated originally, to ask the question of whether it would
Government Orders
it be a reasonable thing, by any member's standards in here, if someone came to you and presented you with a contract in which people said, quite bluntly: "I don't understand this. I have to get somebody to interpret this government document for me." Is it reasonable to expect people to simply accept that? I do not believe it is. I think people have begun now to understand that this is an income tax process, however simple it might have been at the start, which has gone astray.
At the very least, it must be understood by the Canadian people, and it is not. At the very same time, it has to have some large measure of fairness involved in it. The people have to be able to say "Well, I don't like paying taxes either, but I understand we are all paying roughly the same kind of taxation." People certainly are not saying that. They certainly are not saying that.
As one goes through the provision of this bill, one can see the kind of traditional approach which basically says "we have identified a problem over here, and so we addressed the problem over there, and maybe that will solve it". We all have watched this process long enough to know that this is not going to work. It never has worked, it never will work, there is not even a chance that it is going to work.
In conclusion, I am not making a pitch for a flat tax or anything as simple as that, but I am making a pitch that in all fairness the people of Canada should be able to pick up a tax form that is put out by the Government of Canada and read it and understand it, and they cannot. There is something basically wrong with that. There is something basically wrong with the notion that my father, who was 91 years old when he died and had a grade seven education, paid somebody $50 every year to tell him that he did not owe the Government of Canada any income tax. He did that to his dying day. There are millions of Canadians in the same boat who cannot function within the system.
The process, I believe, is clearly wrong. The process seems to be almost impenetrable, there is almost no way that one can break through it. I notice that the ministers who are carrying this bill seem to kind of move around. Nobody wants to stay in the Chamber and defend the faith on this matter, with good reason. It is indefensible and it ought not to be.

Mr. Speaker, I want to thank my colleague from Oshawa for his interesting dissertation. He touched on a couple of points that I know are of some consternation both to myself and many of the constituents I represent.
I think it is the current minister of national health who used to be the minister in charge of nuclear submarines who, when he was in opposition, was the revenue critic for the Conservative Party. He and his party in 1984 and again in 1988, but particularly in 1984, made a great to-do about a campaign to simplify the tax system. I wonder if the member for Oshawa remembers that and if he could perhaps comment a little further on what progress he thinks it may have made in a few ways, if there was any progress, in terms of simplifying that tax system.
Also I would like to comment for a moment and reinforce what my colleague said about the attitude, the Canadian culture, that used to exist that while nobody liked their taxes they paid them. There was some aggravation that perhaps they were paying a little bit more than their fair share, but as long as it was not too burdensome and they could see that their own economic situation was improving however slightly year by year, they were willing to put up with it. It seems to me as it does to my colleague that we are in danger of almost moving into the tax culture of the population in France where people have been making a career for years and years and years now out of tax avoidance. That is the total difference in the whole Canadian culture and attitude toward government, revenue and taxation over the last few years and a very unhealthy one.
My questions are: In what ways, if in any way, has this government since making its major promise to simplify the tax system gone about implementing that? What further comments does my colleague have on the changing tax culture among Canadians and how much more can they take?

Mr. Speaker, in answer to the first question, here is the answer to whether anybody is getting anywhere with the simple application of the Canadian tax system. This one would just choke a horse, and with good reason. This is the kind of legislation in which one minister comes into the House and reads a
very succinct speech on why this is wonderful and then leaves and lets somebody else carry the can. This is indefensible.
I do not want to justify this, but in fairness I think we should acknowledge that the way modem governments operate would swallow anybody's conscience. It chokes them. Around them are people who advise them on things they can say and things they cannot say. Ministers of the Crown are rarely allowed in this place to actually say what they think. They say what is written and no more and no less.
It is that kind of controlling mechanism which is in part causing the problem. I regret that. I regret that people with good intentions in all political parties in my experience have tried to make changes. I think all of us who are practising politicians understand those changes must come. The tragedy is we have not managed to get that message across to those who are supposedly there to serve, to advise, and who have somehow become people who are there to control.
The second question is more disturbing. It is for me because I am of that generation of Canadians who have felt very good about this country and who felt that while I did not ever enjoy in my lifetime paying income tax, I always felt it was my obligation. I always felt there was some fairness somehow in the system that would work itself out and I am beginning to join the ranks of those who are bitter that they are the last ones left on the line so to speak, that they are there to be exploited in large measure by governments at all levels.
That is wrong and it is particularly wrong when I look around in my own community, and everyone of us here could do that, at people who are very well off who pay no income tax. That is a tragedy and I was reminded of that tragedy again in the last little while and this mindset still seems very strong in the Government of Canada. People at the bottom of the process, people who stand at the wickets and face the Canadian public, our civil servants, are expected to take a zero per cent wage increase this year. The government is in this House every day attempting as best it can to articulate why it is absolutely necessary that somebody else who already has a very nice salary needs a substantial bonus and how there is fairness in that.
October 7, 1991

Whatever the legal niceties of that argument might be, the Canadian public looks at that and says words that I am afraid are a little unparliamentary. They do not accept that argument any more. They have sufficient understanding of the process to know that they are the bitter recipients of an income tax system that is wrong.
While they are not exactly sticking their heads out the window, yelling that they are as mad as and are not going to take it any more, I would warrant that they are sitting down at the kitchen table explaining as a family unit how they are being victimized by this process and exploring as many ways as they can to avoid paying their fair share of the income tax. I do not know whether they will be as successful as most of our major corporations, but I will bet that they will give it a try.

Mr. Speaker, I am happy to have the opportunity to rise in this Elouse to speak on Bill C-18, an act to put forward further amendments to the Income Thx Act.
A government's ability to mobilize the will of a nation is based upon trust. Nowhere is the lack of trust more evident in this country than in our current tax system.
The current tax system of Canada with its rules, regulations, exceptions and exceptions to exceptions goes on and on. There is absolutely no way the average person today can fill out his own tax form.
When I was preparing to speak on this bill today I was actually encouraged when I read from the news release from Revenue Canada dated May 24. I noticed the following in the second paragraph: "The fairness package is an important part of my continuing commitment to make the tax system simpler, easier and fairer". This was said by the Minister of National Revenue.
He went on in the third paragraph and talked about how the amendments that would benefit the individual taxpayers in matters such as penalties for late filed returns and interest charged on outstanding balances.
In addition, the fairness package will allow refunds for taxation years starting with 1985 and streamline the process by which individuals can make a formal objection to an assessment issued by the department.
When I read that I was encouraged. Then shortly behind it came Bill C-18. Just the amendments to Bill
Government Orders
C-18 total 400 pages. Today I just took any page and pulled it open. It was page 220, I want to read one paragraph and ask any member of this House if they can honestly decipher it. It is clause 94, the relevant portion of subsection 118.6, and it is talking about qualifying the educational program. Here is how it reads:
The description of A in subsection 118.9(1) of the said Act is
repealed and the following substituted therefor.
This is the amendment, simpler, easier and fairer, and I read:
A is the less of
(a)	$600, and
(b)	the total of all amounts each of which is an amount that the individual may deduct for the year under section 118.6 or an amount that the individual would have been entitled to deduct for the year under subsection 118.5(1) if the reference in paragraph (a) of that subsection to "the amount of any fees for his tuition paid in respect of the year to the educational institution" were read as a reference to "that portion of the individual's fees paid in respect of the year that may reasonably be considered to have been paid in respect of a qualifying educational program of an educational institution described in subparagraph (a)(i) of the definition "designated educational institution" in subsection 118.6(1)"; and
I am not a lawyer and I am not a tax accountant, but I would challenge any tax lawyer or even any tax accountant to tell me what that means.
I agree almost entirely with the hon. member for Oshawa. The current tax system in this country is a disincentive to national productivity. We have been sitting around this House now for many months talking about national productivity. The one instrument that we control in this House that can generate and motivate a positive attitude toward every man, woman and child in this country is the tax system.
Our tax system is so complex, so unfair, so inefficient and so unworkable that there is absolutely no way we have a chance to become a productive nation. The whole system is designed to be a disincentive to productivity.
If we want a mobilized and productive work force we have to treat them fairly. How can we possibly have a work force turned on to what their responsibilities are if they do not understand? Right now it is blind faith in our tax system. What do they read? We read day after day-and we know it to be true-that just two years ago there were close to 7,000 people in this country whose incomes were in excess of $250,000 a year and they paid absolutely no income tax. We heard from Statistics

Government Orders
Canada three years ago that there were 2,200 companies in Canada with retained earnings in excess of $25 million, excluding companies with losses carried forward. Those 2,200 did not pay any taxes at all.
It is not, by the way, that these people who made in excess of $250,000 and did not pay any tax or the companies that did not pay any tax were doing anything illegal. They are working with legal loopholes. These are laws that are written in to the Income Tax Act of Canada which they are naturally working at and they are doing their job.
What an absolute negative energy. Instead of promoting creative ideas on how we can expand our economy, how we can create more jobs, create more wealth, instead of that kind of a thought process, we have high priced chartered accountants and tax lawyers working with negative energy, legitimate ways to avoid tax.
This is no longer just happening in medium sized and larger corporations. The hon. member for Oshawa earlier today cited examples of people coming to his door and saying there is one price if you pay on a credit card or an invoice and there is another price if you pay cash. Now, because of the tax regime of this country, we have an underground economy that goes into the billions of dollars.
Those are not my words, those are the words of Professor W. E. Dewart from the University of British Columbia, who spent many years of his life analysing the underground economy in this country.
I believe that if we are serious about mobilizing the will of this nation, about galvanizing the will of this nation, about creating a productive work force, we have to start by taking dramatic steps to change the tax act for this country.
I have been working with a group of Canadians from coast to coast who believe it is time to do something radical. We believe it is time to come out with a simplified system, something that everyone understands, something that is simple, because from simplicity you can judge fairness, and when you have simplicity and you can judge a system to be fair, efficiencies pick up and this will
cause us to become a nation that will ultimately create better products and services at better prices. This is how the tax act of this country is really a macroeconomic issue.
The hon. member for Oshawa talked earlier about the fact that people sit around in their kitchens or their living-rooms or their backyards, their gas stations or in restaurants and talk about the frustration of the GST, the paper burden of the GST, the complexity of the tax act, the inefficiency of the tax act. They count on us, not only to realize that and hear those words, but they count on us, the people of Canada to do something about it.
I believe the time is now to do something about it. I have been working hard with many other people to promote the idea of a single tax. You could do a single tax idea, Mr. Speaker, on a form that is no bigger than the size of a postcard. There were tax professionals from all over the country who have verified that this is a doable system.
What you basically do, Mr. Speaker, is you take your gross revenue, whether it is personal income or corporate income, whatever form you are working on, and after you take the personal tax credit, the senior's tax credit, child tax credit, charitable donations tax credit, RRSP credits, after you take all of those credits, at the bottom, 20 per cent. If we do that both on the corporate side and the personal side, we will have enough revenue to satisfy the social requirements of governments in this country.
When you have a simplified system which is about the size of a postcard, then people can judge fairness. When people feel they are being treated fairly, they are motivated. They advance. And when foreign investors look at a country and they see a motivated work force, that is when foreign capital moves in.
That is what we need in order to reduce interest rates, in order to put more money into the marketplace for entrepreneurs, to reduce the cost of mortgage rates, cars. Those are the things that expand an economy. When an economy is expanding, and there is a labour force that is working rather than unemployed, those are the things that put downward pressure on deficits and ultimately on the death of the country.

I believe that the only way we are going to get this country back on track is by radical reform of the Income Tax Act of Canada. I know there have been many people who say this idea is off the wall, it is not doable, it is not workable. We are at a crisis point in this country and it is time for the political leadership of this country to take bold measures. It is time for the political will of this country to listen to what is causing people to advance.
The current tax system right now is designed in a way that the harder we work the less we keep. If an entrepreneur in this country decides to work nights and evenings, the harder he or she works the less he or she keeps. It is absolutely upside down.
What is wrong if a person is an achiever, works hard and makes $200,000 or $300,000 a year? We should not have a system that takes nearly half of that. We should not have a system like that. We should not have a system where some of those people can hire very effective tax lawyers and pay absolutely nothing.
The unique thing about a single tax system is that it is an airtight system. Everyone will pay their fair share. No one is exempted. Everyone is in. Legitimate expenses are put on the table, but after that everyone pays their 20 per cent. That is the system.
The current system right now is a disincentive for foreign investment in this country. It is a disincentive to productivity. It does not reward the achievers.
I am happy to have had the opportunity to speak on Bill C-18. The spirit of this government was trying to make things better, but once again the bureaucracy of the Department of Finance wins the day. This bureaucracy in finance-and I realize that it has some of the finest minds in the country-has a self-perpetuating environment in that building.
Can we imagine trying to sell something like a single tax to the Department of Finance which if implemented would probably mean, after a couple of years, about two-thirds of the jobs would have to be reapplied to different departments?
Is it Liberal Party policy, a single tax?

The member asked: "Is it Liberal Party policy?" No, it is not Liberal Party policy, but it is just

one simple idea that is being put forward to try to advance the debate on tax reform.
I will say, seeing as the hon. member asked me, that two weeks ago the Young Liberals of Canada passed it as a priority resolution. That is a beginning.
There are flaws in the single tax system. I know that there can be honest debate on whether or not the tax credits for seniors or the tax credits for children that I am putting forward are too generous. The point is that it is a constructive alternative to the existing system.
Are the members over there against simplicity? Are they against fairness over there? Are they against efficiency? There is not one of the members on the government side who is against those things, not a single member.
When we throw an idea over there-and they have always challenged us-why not take up the challenge? I should say the member for Mississauga South has put forward some concerns about the single tax, and some of his concerns are good concerns. At least it gets an honest debate on tax reform going.
Right now, with respect to the government members, they are all captive. I have worked on that side before. I know how tough this is. They are captive of the officials in the Department of Finance. Whenever they put something forward as a government that is simple and fair, senior officials try to find ways to knock it down. This town is a town that lives on paper. It lives on words.
I appreciate the opportunity to speak on Bill C-18. I continue to hope that there will be a groundswell of caring government members who will eventually challenge the cabinet of Canada, the Prime Minister of Canada, by saying it is not too late to take another fresh start at comprehensive tax reform.

Mr. Speaker, I have a couple of questions in particular for the Liberal member for Broadview-Greenwood. I would like to ask him to take his memory back a few years. I am sure he remembers, as someone who has studied the tax system, that at the end of World War II, the distribution of the tax system in Canada and the tax burden was approximately 75 per cent corporate tax and 25 per cent personal income tax.
