By the end of the Trudeau government in 1984, that situation had totally reversed itself to where it was at that point 75 per cent personal and 15 per cent corporate.
I would like to know how that measures in with his concept of tax fairness.
The other thing is a little more recent, but it is still about 10 years ago. I am sure my colleague will recall the infamous MacEachen budget of 1981 or 1982, in which Allan J. professed at that time that it was his intent with that famous budget to plug loopholes. He did, in fact, plug a number of outrageous corporate loopholes in his proposed budget. At the same time, he also plugged a number of the very few loopholes available to ordinary working Canadians, especially those who worked in northern Canada, who used to get special housing benefits, special fly-in, fly-out benefits-not benefits, but exemptions from taxation for extra cost of living bonuses-in order to make sure they stayed in the north.
At the same time he was proposing to plug all these so-called loopholes, he said: "Well, seeing as we are plugging the corporate loopholes, we will lower the marginal tax rate". There was a chorus of opposition to that budget, because apparently there was no proper consultation. It was not well planned, which always struck me as very unlike the minister's lifetime habit. I had never known him not to plan anything out very carefully. But he lowered the marginal tax rate.
Then there was a chorus of opposition, and he then unplugged all the corporate loopholes again. As far as the loopholes for ordinary workers were concerned, he got rid of those, but he opened up the corporate loopholes. At the same time as he did that, he forgot to reinstate the former marginal tax rate.
What ended up after that entire budget was a taxation system grossly more unfair than that which existed at the beginning.
I am sure the member for Broadview-Greenwood has some recollections of Mr. MacEachen as well. Does he think that kind of action which was supported by the Liberal party, and is still part of the historical record of that party and its financial record of mismanagement in this country, could have really been an accident? Could that have been an accident and not just, instead, typical
of the continuing Liberal record of foisting more and more of the tax burden on to ordinary, working Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, I thank the member for Kootenay West for his question.
On the first point he raised regarding the percentage for corporate income tax at the end of World War II being about 75 per cent, and personal income tax about 25 per cent, he is absolutely correct when he states it is a complete reversal today. It is approximately $49 billion in personal income taxes that go into the national treasuiy today, and about $11 billion from corporate tax. Of that $11 billion, about 80 per cent is made up of mostly small and medium-sized businesses.
I totally disagree with the system as it is today. That is why I am trying to change it and put forward a different approach. I dare to put something on the table which can be challenged and which is certainly less than perfect. It is a conceptual approach at this point, but it has been analysed by the social development model of Statistics Canada.
The main thing is that it is a doable system, in that it will generate the amount of revenue that the Government of Canada needs to meet its requirements. On that point we seem to be in agreement.
On the second point in terms of Mr. MacEachen's budget under my former boss, Mr. Trudeau, I was around at that time and I remember vividly the frustration, the anger that the country exhibited on that honest attempt by Mr. MacEachen to tiy and clean up the system. If I were to say one thing about what I learned from experiencing that exercise and what I have seen subsequently-I mentioned it in my speech earlier today and I am not against the Public Service so please do not take this out of context-it would be that it is very tough to move the officials in the Department of Finance when it comes to cleaning up the Income Thx Act of Canada. I do not think Mr. MacEachen, for whom I have the deepest respect, was tough enough. I do not think he was radical enough in simplifying and making the system more efficient. It was a great attempt but in the process of falling short you end up not advancing any more. That is the point I am making today. I believe that the days of tinkering with the system are over. It is time for a total radical approach.

The president of the Canadian Federation of Independent Business is Mr. Bulloch, or at least I know he used to be the head of it. He probably still is. I know that he

made some criticism concerning the single tax concept, and I would like to know what my colleague's answer is to the criticism by Mr. Bulloch.

Mr. Speaker, Bill C-18 gives us a chance to raise a very important question and I think that the most important thing in a democracy is the way we tax ourselves. I say ourselves, because after all, this government represents the people, and we elect our representatives to reflect the views of all Canadians. However, over the years, we have developed a tax system that has become so complex and so incomprehensible that it takes lawyers specialized in tax law to find ways to save money for big corporations, the wealthy and the financial elite of this country. Look at how thick this volume is! More than 1,400 pages for personal income tax! And so complex it would take someone educated by the Jesuits, and then some, to understand what this is all about. And now, Mr. Speaker, the government wants to introduce amendments-400 pages worth to explain what was not in the document. That gives you some idea of the lack of simplicity and fairness in our tax system.

Government Orders
I imagine the average person and the members of this House realize there is something fundamentally wrong with our tax system. There must be a reason for all these feelings of frustration. The tax system has become so unfair and unjust that people spend a lot of effort, a lot of negative energy, to quote the hon. member to find ways to avoid paying taxes. Our tax system should be simplified to make it not only fair and equitable but also appear to be fair and equitable. However, as long as we have volumes this thick, it certainly does not look like a system that is simple, fair and equitable.
The hon. member mentioned that about ten years ago, a former Minister of Finance, Mr. MacEachen, tried to introduce tax reforms in this House. He was inspired by the findings of a royal commission, the Carter Commission, which was appointed between 1962 and 1963 and existed until 1967. Kenneth Carter, whom I consider a great Canadian, made a thorough study of our tax system and produced a document that was literally revolutionary. It contained some unprecedented elements for a democracy genuinely based on every single group in our society. Our Minister of Finance at the time tried to introduce some of these elements. The hon. member mentioned that this aroused a storm in Canada, but Mr. Speaker, it did not come from the middle class but from the big corporations and the financial community. They saw in this tax reform something that would benefit the middle class. Mr. Speaker, business people obviously take care of their businesses, and it is their business to save as much money as possible. You can hardly blame them. They are not doing anything illegal. In fact, they are well within the law. Here is the law: fourteen hundred pages worth, and another 400 pages of amendments.
Obviously, big companies and financiers can afford to call on lawyers, specialists and tax experts to find ways to pay as little tax as possible. Of course, if this class, the wealthiest in our society, does not pay its fair share, the burden falls on someone else: the middle class, the backbone of our society, indeed the backbone of democracy in all civilized countries. Nevertheless, we in the middle class have had unprecedented tax increases in recent years.
Mr. Speaker, I am not trying to say that our friends opposite, the government, the Conservative Party, are
totally responsible for the tax increases. That is not what I am trying to say. I would like to be fair and equitable by saying that for years, governments have not really managed to find a fair and equitable system. That is the issue before us. They call it a reform, but we are not so gullible as to believe that it is one. What reform has been made in the tax system? Has it been simplified? On the contrary, it is more complex than ever. Does the middle class pay less? The people listening to me, Mr. Speaker, know very well that they pay more than their share. How can it be that millions of Canadians find themselves in a situation where the system has become unfair? Unfortunately, I find that our constituents, especially those in the middle class, cannot afford tax experts, specialists and lawyers to check their income tax returns to see if they are paying $200, $500, $1,000 or $1,500 too much.
In any case, they are too busy earning their living and working every They have other things to do and their purpose in life is not to find out how the tax system works. They take it for granted that those who sit in this House are working in their best interest, but it has been a failure on that score. It was a failure because we do not reflect the real values of our society for the middle class. Is it a great discovery to say that the middle class is the backbone of our society? Let us look at how they are treated.
Mr. Speaker, I was greatly influenced by a book written by Lynda McQuade on the tax system. In French, it is called La part du lion and in English, Behind Closed Doors. I found it extremely interesting because it showed that especially in the last twenty years, the financial elite and big companies have exerted pressure-and I am not saying that they have done anything wrong or illegal- they are looking after their business. They literally had the Department of Finance give them some tax breaks that are to their advantage. It is obvious that is what they did and she shows how it was done. People used to say that the rich don't pay. That's all very well, but if you can't prove it, what can you do? But in her book, she shows how the wealthy in our society were able to benefit under a tax system that was biased in their favour, and there are any number of examples. It's very complex, but it's all there.
October 7, 1991

In recent years, the middle class has started to realize that its tax burden has become intolerable. In the past few years, people have started to realize that we are becoming less and less rich. In other words, the middle class is having trouble maintaining the same standard of living it had in the past.
The sixties and the seventies were years of prosperity. The figures are there, and I am not going to quote Global Economics extensively, but this is an in-depht study which shows that during the sixties, a person earning an average wage could save up to 29 per cent of his net income, to spend on holidays or recreation.
In the seventies, this percentage dropped to around 17 per cent. Today, in the nineties, a member of the middle class who earns an average wage will save less than 1 per cent of his net income.
But what does it all mean? It means that we have to pay more than our share. Obviously, something has to be done.
Mr. Speaker, I was on an open-line show with the local host of a popular radio program, Alain Dexter, who has a wide audience and is very much aware of the way our tax system is biased against the middle class. He called me up and asked me to go on one of his shows to talk to his listeners. It was obvious from what people said that they were completely frustrated and, worst of all, they felt powerless. Although we represent the majority of Canadians and although they elect us, they feel powerless before a tax system that is biased against them.
However, what people must understand is that business people have done nothing unlawful. They take care of their businesses, and their business is to save money. Now that makes sense, doesn't it?
Our role, as middle-class Canadians, is to tell everyone who wants to represent us in this House that changes are required. This bill does not contain any. The middle class is taxed more than ever! What is needed is an in-depth review. We have an advantage over many countries in the world. We had a royal commission, the Carter Commission. We can draw inspiration from it to find ways to tax our people fairly and equitably. And once people will have realized that the fiscal system reflects the social values of integrity and justice, there will be no problem. There is no doubt in my mind that
Government Orders
they will readily accept the fact that there is a deficit which has to be brought down.
I have to congratulate my colleague from Broadview- Greenwood, because everyone here knows how hard he has worked on his single tax concept. His efforts should be recognized. He sought the advice of experts in the field. One of our friends opposite said that there are flaws in his plan, Mr. Speaker. Undoubtedly, and he admitted it himself. However, it is far easier to correct flaws on 2 pages than on 2,000 pages. He made an effort and it was a good way to start the discussions on how to approach the subject. He may not have all the answers, but it is certainly a start because it is by discussing and by submitting ideas- I know that he is aware of the Carter Commission because that was a revolutionary document and he was here then, when the Minister of Finance of the time, Mr. MacEachen, wanted to implement the findings of that commission.
Nothing is easy. It is obvious that everyone wants to protect its own interests. As a former Secretary General to the United Nations once said: "There is no such thing as permanent friends, and there is no such thing as permanent enemies. The only thing that is permanent in this life are personal interests." It is obvious that everybody will fight for that!
But for us the middle class, as well as those who represent it here, our interest is to make sure that the people that we represent are treated in a just and fair manner. That, however, is not the case. They use words such as "reform", but there has not been any reform. And as long as I will have the honour and the privilege to represent the people of the riding of Gatineau-La Lievre in this House, I will work and work and ask the residents in my riding and elsewhere to create a united front. You mau say that everything starts with a dream. The dream that I have is that, at a given time, great numbers of voters will approach all the members of this House to tell them that they are not convinced that this tax system is fair and that they want us the members of Parliament to get on with the task of making sure that it is indeed a fair system.
As I mentioned earlier, there is nothing more fundamental in our society than the tax system. We tax ourselves. If we are incapable of finding a solution, how can we succeed in motivating Canadians to work harder, to keep on paying taxes, and to realize that we live in a

Government Orders
great country, that we enjoy many benefits and that we want to protect them?
Mr. Speaker, what strikes me when I talk to people is their feeling of powerlessness. It really hurts me because the strength of our country is precisely its people. It hurts me to know that workers refuse to work overtime because they say that they pay too much in taxes. What does this mean, Mr. Speaker? They are convinced that they are paying too much in taxes, that is what they are saying. In fact, they feel that they are paying more than their fair share.
Therefore, I ask my voters that, together, we start saying everywhere what we think, and start saying that we are not pleased, that a reform is needed, and that as long as it is not implemented to bring fairness, there is no chance of keeping the social benefits that we enjoy now. We cannot expect the middle class to forever be the milk cow, because those people realize that there is less and less disposable income.
When I hear the Prime Minister say that the recession is over, I wonder since when it is over. We don't have any more money overnight. We have less and less disposable income; that does not change overnight. If the Prime Minister had really wanted to understand what the people go through, and especially the middle class, do you think that he would have imposed a 7 per cent tax just like that? Do you not think, Mr. Speaker, that it could have been imposed gradually, 1 per cent a year for five or six years or 2 per cent a year, to show that an all-out effort was being made to be understanding.
We saw the frustration with the GST. What more do we need to see the deep dissatisfaction in our society with our present system? I will conclude with that, Mr. Speaker. I am not saying that they are to blame for all the problems on earth and in this country-that is not what we are trying to say. But I am trying to say that their attempt is far from convincing and does not tackle the real problem facing our country.
Mr. Speaker, I would like the government to realize that in this House, we all have the same values to defend, regardless of the political parties represented here. We all have the same values to defend. But if we go
on having the same frustrations with the tax system as in the past few months, if we are unable to see something that clear, what hope do we have for the next generation, which sees that a solution cannot be found for a problem that exists and is at the heart of our democracy?

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member says that we all hold to the same values. I think part of the problem is that we do not all hold to the same values. We have different values. That is why we have different political parties and this is a place where we debate which values will actually inform and instruct legislation, in this case the Income Tax Act.
Obviously there is quite a difference in the value system which the hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood employed in his idea of how the tax system should work and the value system which the hon. member for Ottawa South, speaking on behalf of the Liberal Party, brings to his discussion of the taxation system.
On the one hand, we have the hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood defending the idea of a flat tax, a single tax, which we know is particularly associated with him. He has been promoting it for a long time in a constructive way. That is fine, but it is confusing for the people of Canada who are trying to figure out what the Liberal Party stands for in terms of tax reform.
Perhaps the hon. member who just spoke could help us in this regard because, on the one hand, we have the hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood saying: "Everybody, no matter what they make should be taxed the same," and on the other hand, the member for Ottawa South complaining on the same day that one of the problems with the tax system we have now is that in the upper income bracket, everybody is taxed the same, whether you are making $60,000 or $600,000, you are taxed exactly the same.
What we have in the upper income bracket right now is exactly the policy that the member for Broadview- Greenwood is advocating. Yet his colleague, the member for Ottawa South is saying that this is one of the things that is wrong with the tax system.
Perhaps the hon. member who just spoke could explain to us how Liberal policy works. Perhaps he could shed
October 7, 1991

some light on the mystery that surrounds the making of Liberal policy, particularly with respect to tax reform.
It must be very confusing for members opposite and for members on this side to figure out just what is the status of the comments of the hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood. It is one thing to have constructive debate within a party. I am not against that, and I think we should see more of that. If that is all that there is to it, that is fine.
Perhaps he could tell us what the official Liberal position is with respect to the single tax.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member has given us a good example of how complex the law is. He has even managed to confuse other people. We are not discussing policy, we are discussing ideas.
We would like to hear the hon. member's ideas on tax reform. We want to be sure that the tax system is fair and equitable. Is there anything simpler than that? That is what we would like to see. There have been attempts in the past when this particular party was in power to come up with elements that could have made it simpler and more equitable.
We never said it was perfect. We are just discussing ideas. The message that comes through loud and clear, as I mentioned before, is that the middle class in our society is paying more than its fair share. They feel it. They are becoming more and more outspoken, and I think that it is time that we addressed the whole problem. We are listening to all ideas. Our friend from Broadview-Greenwood brought up an idea, the single tax. It certainly has a lot of merit and has been discussed in many quarters, but it is one of the ideas that is probably going to bring us in time to what I hope to be a truly fair and equitable tax system and we certainly have not seen it yet.

Mr. Speaker, if the hon. member who spoke a few moments ago from the NDP is interested in what the Liberal Party is going to do, he should listen to the member for Gatineau who just spoke and read the writings of the hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood who has written so many papers, books, and everything. He spent days, nights, and months writing. The hon. member should read some of his writings and listen to the hon. member for Gatineau.
Government Orders
I want to ask a question in the form of a comment. Every time I have listened to the hon. member, and I have heard him over the years-I heard him in another assembly speaking about this subject of taxation as it relates to the middle class-he has always proposed in his speeches before today that the middle class must organize itself to become more effective in the political system vis-a-vis tax reform. Could the hon. member elaborate on that statement he has always made?

Mr. Speaker, that is probably the biggest task we have before us. There is so much information out there and it is so complex. You can imagine the average citizen when he sees volumes of this size. Nobody wants to be ridiculed. Can you imagine trying to wade through this and finding an answer?
Obviously we have to find a simpler way. That is what we have been hearing from our people and our electors who form the middle class. They do not want to go into it page by page and the bits behind it. They know they would be lost in no time and they could be ridiculed. Nobody likes to be ridiculed. But they understand one fundamental thing: they are paying more than their fair share. The odd time they read about people earning more than $100,000 or so and not paying any income tax. People having write-offs, multinational companies- there is no end to it.
How can they be indifferent? They are upset and as I mentioned they feel powerless. The middle class needs to get organized.
Obviously I have been in contact with different organizations. They are ready to take up the battle and I know that it is going to take time. In my area there are going to be more groups paying visits to candidates in the next federal election, and they are going to ask, not in 50 or 400 pages, it is going to be one page, how candidates feel about the tax system and where they stand on reform that will be fair and equitable to all Canadians, and that will not be easy to achieve.
In this political system when the different candidates see that the majority want an answer to a problem like that and they see that the electorate is concerned, we will get answers from the members who will be sitting here after that election.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member talks about people coming to members wanting to know where they stand. That is precisely what I want to know from him, where he stands with respect to a discrepancy between what the hon. member for Broad-

October 7, 1991
Government Orders
view-Greenwood had to say and what the hon. member for Ottawa South had to say and he gets up and tells me they are just talking about ideas, not policies.
First of all, maybe he could tell me the difference between an idea and a policy' because it seems to me they are intimately related. Second, he could maybe give some answers on behalf of the Liberal Party. What is its policy or idea with respect, for instance, to the GST? Can he get up and say unequivocally that the Liberal Party will get rid of the GST if it comes into office? That is the kind of thing that people want to know from their political parties.

Mr. Speaker, that is an example of a member of this House who, instead of advancing the debate, is trying to find all sorts of "holes" and wondering what will happen if we give up something for something else. Is that really constructive? We are trying to find a complete answer.
He talks about values!

Mr. Speaker, we are trying to advance the debate. Of course, it would be easy for any opposition party to say that it would abolish this or that, as we saw in the past. We just want to point out that it is in the interest of most Canadians to have a thorough study of our tax system done. Saying that you will abolish the GST will not solve the problem. It will not solve the problem, which is much deeper than that!

Mr. Speaker, I too want to join in the debate on the changes to the income tax and other legislation. Later on I will be dealing with one of the proposals in the legislation, the northern tax allowance, and how that is introduced into this legislation.
First let me talk about the policy of the New Democratic Party with regard to taxation versus the policy of the two members who spoke before me on behalf of the Liberal Party. I listened to the two members speak. I tend to forget that they were the government for most of the time since World War II and that the discrepancies and the inherent discrimination that exists within our taxation system is not only as a result of the last seven
years of Conservative rule, but is basically as a result of the taxation system that the Liberal Party of Canada put into place.
The present Leader of the Liberal Party, Mr. Chretien, the former Leader of the Liberal Party, Mr. Turner, were both ministers of finance. When they were not members of Parliament they were both corporate lawyers sitting on various boards of directors. They received, as we all know, much of their campaign funds from corporations. We have to wonder how a Liberal member in this House can get up and say: "It is true that in 1949, about 75 per cent of the income tax came from corporations and only about 25 per cent came from individuals". Then the hon. member said: "Of course, that is changed now." It is true that individuals pay about three-quarters of the income tax and actually much more than three-quarters and yet corporations only pay the smaller percentage. He said: "It is true that of the percentage that is paid by corporations, it is the small businesses that are paying the lion's share of it, not the large profitable corporations".
Where are the New Democratic Party ideas?

Mr. Speaker, take a look at what has happened in this country. We know there was that old line: Who pays more income tax, the bank clerk with the salary of $15,000 or $18,000 or $20,000 a year of the bank? And Canadians knew what the answer was. It was the bank clerk who paid more in income tax.
I find it ironic today that the Liberals have a speaker get up and say one thing, and another Liberal getting up and saying a different thing. That is so typical, because the members of the Liberal Party do not have a policy when they are in opposition. They have many different ideas, but they do not tell Canadians where they stand. Somehow they forget that their leaders, the present leader and the previous leader, were ministers of finance who helped to create the very system that is a problem today. There is example after example of how corporations have not paid their fair share of taxes.
Someone asked, where are the New Democratic Party ideas? We do not have to only quote from the policy papers that we have put forward in opposition to the GST, where all members of this House know we were the only party that gave specific examples of how we would raise taxes in this country as opposed to having the GST.

We gave examples and we had no fear about sending our report out to Canadians. Thousands of Canadians asked for that report and we sent it out. That was a party document, that was not the document of one individual. We explained our policy, whereas the Liberals as usual were ducking. That is what happened with the Liberals.
As I was pointing out, it is not a new idea. It is not new for the New Democratic Party to say that there are problems with the tax system. It is not new for us to say, as the Liberal member for Broadview-Greenwood is now saying, that the corporations are not paying their fair share of taxes. It was 19 years ago when our previous leader, the late David Lewis, wrote his book on corporate welfare bums The Louder Ibices. The louder voices in our society had the ear of government. They had the ear of the elected representatives, again basically of the Liberal Party, but they also had the ear of the bureaucratic elite within our society.
In other words, the 1,400 pages that form the Income Thx Act today are a result of those louder voices. The 400 pages that we have in front of us as amendments to the legislation are again a result of those agencies within our society that have the louder voices.
As usual, scattered among that Income Tax Act and scattered among the 400 pages, there are a few good ideas that will help the disabled and that will help people in some northern communities. There are always some good ideas, some ideas that help the ordinary Canadian. However, by and large the changes in our taxation policy have not benefited ordinary Canadians.
It reminds me of the debate we had in the House of Commons earlier on the Public Service Alliance strike where it was said that people at the top would get zero and people at the bottom would get zero and that seemed fair. Then we found out that a whole bunch of other things were happening like bonuses and all sorts of performance pay so that the people at the top were still going to get more.
What has happened in our society is that the people at the top have always been getting more, whether we have a 0 per cent wage increase in place or whatever because there seems to be a different set of values, a different set
Government Orders
of beliefs in how we should treat those at the top and how we should treat regular, ordinary Canadians. Somehow it has always been okay for corporations to have the three martini lunch and have that written off as a tax expenditure. Somehow it has always been okay for those in business to have a second family car and pretend it is a business car. It has always been okay for certain of their vacation costs to be covered by taxation. That seems to be an accepted belief within the government parties.
Governments have always written the taxation laws in such a way that a working Canadian on a regular salary is always going to be paying much more than his or her fair share of taxes, but those who run corporations, those who are at the top of the corporate ladder, those who are at the top of the government bureaucratic ladder, are going to have all sorts of benefits that are not taxed. That is a problem within the taxation system.
There are good ideas that can help alleviate that, but we have to understand that unless a political party is actually going to stand up and have its leader say that that is its policy it really means very little. It means very little when we know that the leader of the particular party has instigated a lot of the discrepancies and problems in our taxation system. It is very interesting to know that. It is very interesting to know that it is not just one, but it is a number of the Liberal leaders who have actually been behind the taxation system in this country at this time.
It is unfortunate that the Liberal Party does not have any ideas as a corporate whole and that it has to say: "We have somebody over here with a good idea on taxation and on human rights". That person over there might have some good ideas as a Liberal on human rights. That person speaks for the Liberals but he really does not speak for them on aboriginal affairs.
Oh, oh.

The Liberals get upset when that is pointed out. I point that out, not only to criticize the Liberal Party, but because that is the exact problem we have with the present Prime Minister and the Conservative Party.

Government Orders
Remember the famous line of the hon. member for St. John's West: "If we told you what we would do, you would never vote for us". That was the Conservative line. They did not want to say what their policy was. They too had a strategy. Somebody over here would be saying: "We should have a simple income tax system". This is not a new idea. We used to have Conservative backbenchers giving the same suggestion, but it was never Conservative Party policy. It certainly was never taken up by the Conservative leadership.
There are problems in our taxation system. We do know that corporations are not paying their fair share of taxes and that we have created a system which is so complicated that it can never be fair.
It is ironic that we have had government after government, Minister of Finance after Minister of Finance getting up and saying: "I have proposals here which will make the taxation system simpler". Well, it ain't simple and it is not getting simpler.
Let me give an example, as it relates to the bill, of how complicated government has made taxation. When I was elected in 1979 there were certain benefits that people in the north received which were not taxed. Then as part of the MacEachen budget that was referred to earlier, it was decided to tax some of those benefits.
Then some people said: "Maybe that is not right". So all together we had three different years of moratorium on the taxation of northern benefits. That took us through the first six years of the period when I was elected.
Then the Conservatives came in and they decided they were going to have a northern tax allowance, but they would tax those things like housing, free travel to and from remote communities. They were going to have a northern tax allowance and that would resolve the problem.
Then two years later, after the government made that decision, the Minister of Finance came down with some new criteria which would take away 134 communities that used to receive northern benefits. While he was cutting these northern communities, he added communities to the northern tax allowance system that were bordering on the United States. I am not talking about the Yukon-Alaska border. I am talking about the
border that comes around the 49th parallel. There was another system coming in from government.
A number of communities, including the communities of Thompson and Wabowden in my riding, were quite upset. They were not northern communities, but communities down south all of a sudden were northern communities.
The minister set up a task force with a mandate to come up with a northern benefit system that would be fair and would neither increase nor decrease revenue from the federal government. The commission went out and held hearings for a couple of years. Then after they had finished holding hearings the former Minister of Finance, now the Minister for International Trade, changed the guidelines for that committee. He said it was okay if it came down with a set of packages that may increase or may decrease revenue. Before it had hearings it was told to be basically revenue neutral. Then it had three years of hearings and the guidelines were changed so it could come down with a report which would in effect increase revenue.
That is exactly what the task force did. This task force came down in the fall of 1989 and recommended a procedure that would have created a situation whereby 2,740 communities would lose their benefit.
Obviously that created a bit of a problem for the government because a lot of those communities were in northern Tory ridings. A year later, they decided that idea was not a good one, so they have people coming to government and saying well, we want to change that, we want to change this. So the government came down last December and decided that we will not have one zone for northern tax benefits, we will have two zones. They drew a map and they had it presented and you know what? The idea in itself may have some benefit, but they drew these lines across the country. There is no appeal process, and some of the clauses in the legislation in front of us today basically enables this new process come into place.
Let me give an example of what has happened. Little Grand Rapids is a community in my constituency. It is hundreds of miles from any roads. It does not have a railway, it does not have ships. We are talking basically about a community where everything has to be flown in, or where you need to have winter roads. That is considered to be in the intermediate zone. In other
October 7, 1991

words, it does not receive a full northern tax benefit, but only a 50 per cent tax benefit.
Another community which does not have roads, which does not have any regular access, the community of Bloodvein, is not even considered. This community does not receive any northern tax allowance.
The bureaucrats in Finance came across with a good idea in terms of setting out two different criteria, recognizing that some of the communities should receive 100 per cent northern tax benefit and others should receive a lesser percentage; 50 per cent was the suggestion made here.
But they do not allow for the people to really explain what the situation is. How do you feel if you are in a community in northern Manitoba, northern B.C., northern Saskatchewan or northern Ontario. You do not have any roads, and you are told you are not in a northern community.
I have raised the issue of northern tax benefits more often in this House than any other member. I have had to do so for the last 12 years that I have been a member of Parliament. One of the problems is not the fact that there is a northern tax benefit. The problem is that no one is really listening to the people who live in those communities. That is a specific problem that I felt should be addressed with regard to the legislation.
I think that same problem exists with a lot of other clauses in the Income Tax Act. It always seems that the louder voices are listened to, that the corporations can make the Minister of Finance believe that the three-martini lunch is a reasonable tax write-off because that is necessary to promote business.
We know of all sorts of people who run around making sure they pretend to pay the bill at the end of every lunch so they can write it off as a tax expenditure.
Ordinary Canadians who have to go out and buy tools in order to practise their livelihood are told: "No, you cannot write that off as an expense. What do you need tools for? What do you mean you are a carpenter? You are a welder. Why do you have to buy this equipment?" It may be stipulated in your job description that you need this equipment, but you cannot write it off as a tax expenditure. Now, if that person could go out, he or she
Government Orders
could probably quite successfully explain why she had to have three martinis for lunch and have that written off as a tax exemption, but not the tools they need for their trade.
It points out the real problem in our tax system, and that is, who is being listened to? Until we find a way to make sure that corporations pay their fair share of taxes, to make sure that expenses are really business related expenses, we are not going to have any fairness in our taxation system.
A single tax may sound attractive to many people, but that is not going to resolve any issues as long as corporations are in a position to declare certain things as regular reasonable business expenses that we know are not really business expenses.
That is the problem, there is no fairness in the system. There is no desire by this government or by previous governments to be fair in the taxation system. There is no policy by the Liberal Party to have a simple, fair taxation system. There is certainly no policy by this Conservative government that gives us a fair and simple taxation system. It goes against their corporate interests.
There is no doubt that there are many people in this society who do not want a fair tax system. It means that the very people on top of the ladder, those in charge of corporations, are going to have to pay more. They know that, and they do not want a fair taxation system. They will ensure that we do not have a fair taxation system in this country.
Unfortunately, as long as the Liberals and the Conservatives are beholden to the corporate elite in this society, they are not going to change the taxation system in this country.

Mr. Speaker, I listened attentively to the member from the New Democratic Party for the last 20 minutes.
He talked about different ideas that we were trying to put forward in order to advance the debate on the tax condition in this country.
I noticed that not once did he put forward a specific idea of the New Democratic Party or, for that matter, from his own riding.

October 7, 1991
Adjournment Debate
I campaigned in the last election against the New Democratic Party. If there is one thing that I noticed it is that people in Canada are fed up with listening to politicians who just oppose for the sake of opposing. They want to hear constructive ideas and alternatives.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be able to utilize the following few minutes available to me to revisit a question I asked on September 23, 1991 of the Minister of Transport with regard to the open skies negotiations with United States of America.
We all know the troubling times that the aviation industry is going through. There were some 3,000 people laid off last summer as you will no doubt recall between Air Canada and Canadian. A few weeks ago, there were another 2,300 people laid off between Air Canada, Canadian and Nationair.
The suggestion is that we ought to make the industry stronger, that we have to right the wrongs and we have to try to establish a strong foundation for a domestic airline industry. It seems to me that this government, going into the open skies negotiations, with suggestions that we are going to get cabotage, which is a fancy code word that says that any American carrier can travel freely across Canada to pick up passengers and drop them off at any point, and therefore compete openly with our domestic carriers.
That will not make an industry stronger, but in fact push not only Air Canada and Canadian probably to merge, but in a number of years, without sounding alarmist, I do not think we will speaking of a Canadian-owned, Canadian-controlled industry.
When this government gave us deregulation in the air, promised diversification and greater competition, meaning better prices for Canadians and meaning more competitiveness in the private sector.
What we have in essence is a duopoly. What happened to all the regional air carriers, the commuter services that were basically gobbled up by the two air carriers, Air Canada and Canadian. In the open skies negotiations, if we give the Americans carte blanche to do to Canadian and Air Canada what Air Canada and Canadian did, with all due respect, to the regional airlines, then I think the conclusion and the net result are quite predictable.
Therefore, I and other colleagues of this side of the House have been asking the government for a clear assurance, a clear commitment that in the open skies negotiations the Canadian negotiating side would not give in as our side gave in during the free trade talks to granting Americans cabotage rights. That is to say, we are in favour of trying to bring the agreement which has been last visited in 1974 up to speed. We are prepared to take a look at various parts of the industry. However, we are not prepared to completely deregulate the industry. We still wish to deregulate it and we still wish to protect our carriers in the face of the giant American carriers. We do not want to do in the air what this government has done to the truckers on the ground.
Therefore we ask the government for a clear undertaking that there will be no cabotage at the end of the negotiations. If there was a choice between cabotage and breaking off the negotiations, this side would be in favour of the latter in respect of our industry and the realities they are in. The minister did not want to answer in a clear concise way, and I am hopeful and am looking forward to the relatively new parliamentary secretary, who has had a fairly auspicious start, who has been fairly co-operative, to perhaps clarify the situation today for Canadians in favour of a Canadian domestic industry.

Mr. Speaker, I am glad that the hon. member opposite has given me an opportunity again to put the position of the government on the record.
The approach taken by Canada at the bilateral air negotiations with the United States takes into full
October 7, 1991

account the financial state and the needs of the Canadian airline industry.
At the exploratory rounds held to date, Canadian negotiators have repeatedly emphasized to the U.S. that any new agreement must include a phased approach to implementation and meaningful safeguards to provide conditions that will ensure the ongoing viability of the Canadian airline industry.
These negotiations have included a consultation process that is unprecedented in scope for bilateral air negotiations. The Canadian delegation at the negotiations includes representatives of the airlines, unions and communities. Their views are given full consideration in the Canadian negotiating position.
There is no intention on the part of Canada to give U.S. carriers access to Canada in a manner that would be to the detriment of the Canadian industry, as suggested by the opposition member.
The issue of cabotage has been greatly over-emphasized. Canada will not negotiate cabotage or any other right unless it represents a good deal for Canadian carriers and does not threaten their viability or the preservation of Canada's air transportation system.
As my hon. friend also knows, there are many other important issues to be taken into account such as fair and competitive access to U.S. airports and advantages for Canadian carriers to offset U.S. carrier strengths. All of these have to be addressed so that we end up with a good deal for Canadian carriers and for Canadian users of trans-border air services.

10.5	per cent. Today unemployment has gone up, in spite of the fact that this government claims the recession is over. Unemployment is now at 10.6 per cent.
Adjournment Debate
In my area of metropolitan Toronto, unemployment is at 10.8 per cent, above the national average. Toronto used to be the industrial heartland of Canada.
What is happening? This government's policies of giving us free trade and at the same time increasing the value of our dollar by 20 per cent, increasing our interest rates, increasing our tax levels, has driven businesses out of business. It has caused bankruptcies. Thirteen per cent of Canadian manufacturing jobs have been lost in Canada since free trade came in due to this government's economic mismanagement. Two hundred and sixty-one thousand manufacturing jobs have been lost. If this recession ends, many of those jobs will not come back. Sixty to seventy per cent of them are gone forever. The ones that were not just wiped off the map have moved south to the United States.
Why is this? It is because this government has been totally oblivious to the needs of our Canadian industries and what it takes to make our industries competitive and strong.
What is even more alarming is not just the number of jobs we have lost today, but ask anybody in this country who is putting up new industrial plants, who is building new factories. No one. They are just not there.
Is the mood turning around now that the recession is supposedly over? The Canadian Federation for Independent Business revealed in a survey that 36 per cent of small and medium-sized businesses in Ontario are considering moving out with a potential job loss of 500,000 jobs.
We see something that is happening at de Havilland, metro Toronto's biggest industrial employer; 4,200 workers today, announced layoffs of 1,300, plus a threat to close the plant. Will this government give us one firm commitment that it is prepared to stand behind de Havilland and its workers, a leading aerospace industry in the world, producer of the best commuter aircraft of its class in the world?
This government's economic mismanagement has not only driven jobs out of this country, it is continuing to drive those jobs out, and business has lost confidence in this government.
Dramatic measures are necessary and it means a complete reversal of this government's policies, not just

Adjournment Debate
for my province, but right across this country, or otherwise this ruination, this deindustrialization and this transformation of Canada from a branch plant into a warehouse economy will continue.

Mr. Speaker, elaborating on my question of September 30, why do we need greater support for multiculturalism in Canada?
This past summer we witnessed acts of racial violence against black Canadians in Halifax and Montreal. Continuing injustices against native Canadians were documented in the Manitoba aboriginal justice inquiry.
Last week I reported on discrimination against persons of colour at Canadian border crossings. Today we read that the Solicitor General of Canada defends the use of ethnic crime data which is contrary to sound human rights practices and will increase racial stereotyping.
Employment equity is not enforced by the federal government and racial minorities do not have equal opportunities for employment and promotion.
While racism escalates and systemic discrimination continues, we have also heard a growing backlash against multiculturalism, particularly against the new Department of Multiculturalism and Citizenship.
The Spicer report illustrated a lack of public understanding of multiculturalism, although its recommendations for a review and for closer co-ordination with immigration and settlement were appropriate.
The Reform Party advocates discontinuation of multiculturalism altogether and funding of multicultural programs. Not to be out-reformed, the delegates to the Conservative Party convention voted unanimously to do away with the Department of Multiculturalism and all funding for multicultural organizations.
Tory resolutions called for the abandonment of multiculturalism in favour of a melting pot policy, restrictions on where new immigrants can live and restrictions on citizenship to require five years of residency.
Canadians deserve to know whether the Prime Minister and his government will follow these Conservative Party policy decisions. Will funding for programs to fight racism be cut? Will advocacy groups that speak for minorities be refused funds? Will obligations on the
Multiculturalism Act be abandoned? Will employment equity for visible minorities continue to be ignored?
On September 30, in the absence of the Prime Minister, the Minister of Multiculturalism replied to my question, defending his department and in particular his priority of working to combat racism.
I appreciate his sincerity but must insist that to be effective multiculturalism policy must have strong support from the Prime Minister and cabinet to become a government priority. The early examples I have cited prove how far we have yet to go.
I also asked the minister to undertake a major public education program to promote a better understanding of multiculturalism.
I did not mean just the programs undertaken on March 21, the international day to counteract racism. We need a revision of Canadian history books to reflect accurately ethnic history. We need to enlist actively the support of the media which too often add to stereotyping and hysteria. We need thoughtful public discussions about the changing nature of Canada, our multicultural heritage, our appreciation of diversity, and our national commitment to protect minority rights.
As Canadians reconsider our future, we must have full participation of persons and groups from all ethnic origins. Multiculturalism is not just for ethnic minorities. It reflects the very nature of our citizenship and our national values. Recognition of this fact must be reflected in all aspects of government and in public policies.

Mr. Speaker, given the time available, I will try also to give my colleague as comprehensive an answer as possible. First of all I would like to stress that the hon. member for Vancouver is supporting the eradication of racial discrimination in Canada. I would like to point out to her that there is a big difference between the preliminary resolution, passed by delegates at the last Conservative convention and the actual policy of the government. Indeed, the constitutional proposals recent-

ly tabled in the House confirm the government's strong commitment to equal participation, common citizenship and national unity.
The federal government is determined to play a leading role in the eradication of racism and racial discrimination in this country. However, this is a task which it cannot carry out alone. We need the cooperation of all Canadians, all government organizations as well as the private sector if we want to achieve progress in eliminating barriers to equality and full participation in our society. That is the reason why, Mr. Speaker, last summer, following some incidents in Halifax and Montreal which increased racial tensions, the Minister of Multiculturalism and Citizenship set up in Nova Scotia an Advisory Committee on Race Relations.
This advisory committee, made up of representatives from all three government levels and the black community, had the mandate to come up with an action plan and make recommendations to fight racism. In thirty days, the advisory group was able to write a report which they presented to the Minister of Multiculturalism and Citizenship on September 11. That is an excellent example of what we can achieve by working together.
Mr. Speaker, Canada continues to act on the basic principles mentioned in the Canadian Multiculturalism Act. I would like to point out some of the initiatives taken so far, such as the creation of the Canadian Centre on Policing and Race Relation. That centre seeks to improve relations between the police and various cultural groups in Canada.
I would like to continue, Mr. Speaker, but I can see my time is up.

Mr. Speaker, on October 25, I put a question to the Minister of State for Grains and Oilseeds concerning the financial disaster which is facing Canadian farmers. I pointed out to the minister that spontaneous rallies were being held across the country, from Lucknow, Ontario to Miami, Manitoba to Russell, Manitoba to Rosetown, Saskatchewan and right across the country.
I put this question to the minister: How much longer do farmers have to continue to rally? How much longer
Adjournment Debate
do they have to continue to lose their farms? How much longer do their families, their livelihood, their integrity as farmers in rural Canada have to be put under this kind of sledge-hammer action by the government before there will be action?
It was very interesting that when the minister replied he said: "You would think that the whole problem is the result of this government's policy". That is exactly the problem. The government provided very extensive support to farmers in 1987, 1988 and 1989.
We will recall that 1988 was an election year. What we are concerned about is the way the government dramatically chopped support last year. It cut support across this country to Canadian farmers by $1.3 billion, approximately $1 billion in western Canada and $300 million in eastern Canada.
At the same time that this government was chopping support to Canadian farmers, the value of their grain was dropping by some 30 per cent from roughly $135 a tonne for wheat to about $95 a tonne for wheat.
This spring the government brought in a new safety net program. Generally farm groups were saying they supported the safety net program with one proviso. Because of the government's cutback in support last year on the 1990 crop, they were asking that there be special, transitional support this past spring. In the west they talked in terms of $1 billion. In eastern Canada they talked in terms of $200 million.
What we have seen since that legislation was passed is a series of non-cash assistance. In fact, no cash significance of any amount has been provided since last spring. That is why we are seeing momentous rallies forming all over this country. This is why farmers tell us they are in the worst financial crisis in living memory, because of the price of wheat, because the government has welshed on its commitment to provide that emergency cash transitional assistance.
The most maddening part of it is that we hear all kinds of smoke screens as to why it is not doing this. It is consulting with the third line of defence. The Prime Minister threw out a tidbit last week in Winnipeg that he is considering it. He is asking for a recommendation.

Adjournment Debate
The fanners have been asking, simple and plain, since last March and April: "There is a crisis on our hands. If you don't do something there is going to be a desperate situation". Canadian farmers are facing that desperate situation now. They want action by this government.

speakeroldname: Mr. Murray Cardiff (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is an honour to be able to respond to the hon. member for Algoma. I want to say that this government has always supported our farmers and will support our farmers in this great nation of Canada. To have someone say that we have not is just not the case at all.
GRIP and NISA were developed at the request of producers to replace a system of ad hoc payments. That is what it was over the last few years, just ad hoc payments to deal with a situation that is not predictable. How can a farmer go to the bank with a program like that?
That is the reason the safety nets were put in place. They are bankable programs. Before you plant a crop you can go to your lending institution and get the support that is necessary to plant that crop.
Also, because of those safety net programs, over the next 12 months approximately $2 billion will be delivered to farmers through these programs. That assistance will be most helpful, I know. No matter what the hon. member for Algoma says, $2 billion is a lot of money. As someone said in the House today: "That is not chicken feed".
We know there continues to be hurt out there. There is no getting away from that. We are committed to doing the very best that we can to support our farmers through this very difficult time. The fact is that the government has been there for Canadian farmers, as I said before. As I said, our record of support for agriculture is unprecedented.
Just last Friday the Prime Minister met with farm leaders in Winnipeg to listen to their concerns but, more important, what the Prime Minister did at that time was he gave his commitment that further cash assistance would be forthcoming. The Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of State for Grains and Oilseeds will be reporting their findings and recommendations to the Prime Minister by the end of this week.
We will then be able to respond to the needs expressed by the farm leaders throughout Canada. That is part of the established program that is there to work with the farm leaders in this country to deliver the programs as are needed.
We will still continue to pursue our efforts through the GATT agreement and the negotiations that are taking place there. I just want to reinforce that this government does support our agricultural industry in this country. [Translation]
